context:
##### Iterative pruning {#sec-model-compression-iterative-pruning-ee12}

Iterative pruning removes capacity gradually, alternating each structural cut with fine-tuning so that the network recovers before the next cut. Across three successive prune-and-retrain cycles, accuracy drops after each cut and recovers during the fine-tuning that follows (@fig-iterative-pruning).

title: Illustrative One-Shot Pruning Impact
caption: **Illustrative One-Shot Pruning Impact**: All six channels (27 percent) are removed simultaneously, causing accuracy to drop from 0.995 to 0.914. Fine-tuning recovers only to 0.943, a 5 percent degradation from the original accuracy.
alt: Single-row workflow showing one-shot pruning. CNN with six red-highlighted channels to prune, followed by accuracy drop from 0.995 to 0.914, fine-tuning gears, and partial recovery to 0.943.
context:
**One-shot pruning**\index{One-shot pruning!definition} removes multiple architectural components in a single step, followed by an extensive fine-tuning phase to recover model accuracy. This aggressive approach compresses the model quickly but risks greater accuracy degradation, as the network must adapt to significant structural changes simultaneously.

Applying one-shot pruning to the same network illustrates the hazard of aggressive structural truncation. Excising all six highlighted channels simultaneously (@fig-oneshot-pruning) precipitates a sudden accuracy plunge from 0.995 to 0.914, from which fine-tuning recovers only partially to 0.943, leaving about a 5 percent quality penalty under the recovery procedure shown. The two figures illustrate a mechanism, not a controlled result. Both runs end with the same tensor geometry, but the iterative run also received three rounds of fine-tuning, so its better final accuracy mixes the benefit of smaller cuts with the benefit of more recovery training. A fair comparison holds the final structure and the total recovery budget fixed.

title: Lottery Ticket Iteration Cycle
caption: **Lottery Ticket Iteration Cycle**: The original procedure repeatedly trains, prunes low-magnitude weights, and resets surviving weights to their initial state $\ModelParameters_0$. The cycle tests whether the resulting sparse subnetwork can match the dense baseline when trained in isolation; the outcome is empirical rather than guaranteed.
alt: Left, a flowchart starts at randomly initialize the weights and then cycles through train the network until convergence, prune a percentage of the lowest weights, and reset weights to initial values, with the loop labeled Iterate. Right, a dense network diagram highlights in red the surviving neurons and connections, labeled as the winning lottery ticket subnetwork.
context:
[^fn-lottery-ticket-sparsity]: **Lottery ticket hypothesis**\index{Lottery ticket hypothesis!etymology}: Named for the intuition that training a large network is like buying many lottery tickets, most of which lose, while a few "winning tickets" (sparse subnetworks with favorable initializations) can train to comparable accuracy on their own. @frankle2019lottery established the hypothesis on smaller vision and fully connected networks; later work surveyed and extended the idea to larger settings [@rachwan2022winning]. The systems implication is that some of the memory and compute spent training dense networks may be discoverable overhead, but the practical payoff depends on whether the winning subnetwork can be found before paying most of the original training cost.

The discovery procedure is an iterative pruning-and-rewinding loop. After training to convergence and pruning low-magnitude connections, the surviving weights reset to their initialization state $\ModelParameters_0$, which isolates a sparse subnetwork (@fig-winning-ticket). Repeating the cycle can isolate a sparse subnetwork that, in the reported settings, trains to accuracy comparable with the original network [@frankle2019lottery]. Whether the same procedure succeeds depends on architecture, scale, optimizer, and training budget.

title: Low-Rank Factorization
caption: **Low-Rank Factorization**: A weight matrix $\WeightMatrix$ of size $\WeightMatrixRowCount{\times}\WeightMatrixColumnCount$ is approximated by two smaller factors, $\LowRankLeftFactor$ $(\WeightMatrixRowCount{\times}\FactorizationRank)$ and $\LowRankRightFactor^T$ $(\FactorizationRank{\times}\WeightMatrixColumnCount)$. Storage falls from $\WeightMatrixRowCount \times \WeightMatrixColumnCount$ to $\WeightMatrixRowCount \times \FactorizationRank + \FactorizationRank \times \WeightMatrixColumnCount$ parameters, while one dense operation becomes two factor operations.
alt: Three rectangular boxes show matrix factorization. A large W matrix of size m by n approximately equals the product of a narrower U matrix of size m by k and a wider V-transpose matrix of size k by n.

title: Tensor Decomposition
caption: **Tensor Decomposition**: A three-dimensional tensor $\DecomposedTensor\in\mathbb{R}^{\TensorRowModeSize{\times}\TensorColumnModeSize{\times}\TensorDepthModeSize}$ is approximated by factor matrices $\RowModeFactorMatrix$, $\ColumnModeFactorMatrix$, and $\DepthModeFactorMatrix$. The highlighted factor vectors $\RowModeFactorSlice_i$, $\ColumnModeFactorSlice_j$, and $\DepthModeFactorSlice_t$ combine across rank $\FactorizationRank$ to reconstruct the entry $\DecomposedTensorEntry$. Extending low-rank approximation from two dimensions to three carries the storage and computation argument into convolutional layers. Source: [@gholami2022].
alt: A three-dimensional tensor Y with dimensions I by J by T beside factor matrices A, transposed B, and C. Highlighted factor vectors a i, b j, and c t combine across the rank dimension to reconstruct tensor entry y i j t.
context:
#### Tensor decomposition (optional depth) {#sec-model-compression-tensor-decomposition-5e9e}

**Tensor decomposition**\index{Tensor decomposition!definition} extends low-rank approximation to multidimensional arrays, such as four-dimensional convolutional kernels ($\LayerOutputWidth \times \LayerInputWidth \times \KernelHeight \times \KernelWidth$) and multi-head attention weights. Matrix factorization could compress such a tensor only after unfolding it into a matrix, which discards which axis was which. Tensor decompositions instead keep each axis separate by representing the tensor through multilinear products of lower-dimensional factors. A three-dimensional tensor $\DecomposedTensor\in \mathbb{R}^{\TensorRowModeSize\times \TensorColumnModeSize\times \TensorDepthModeSize}$, for example, decomposes into three rank-$\FactorizationRank$ factor matrices ($\RowModeFactorMatrix$, $\ColumnModeFactorMatrix$, and $\DepthModeFactorMatrix$), and outer products of the slice vectors $\RowModeFactorSlice_i$, $\ColumnModeFactorSlice_j$, and $\DepthModeFactorSlice_t$ reconstruct entry $\DecomposedTensorEntry$ (@fig-tensor-decomposition).

title: Soft Target Distribution
caption: **Soft Target Distribution**: The teacher's relative confidence levels indicate which classes are semantically similar (for example, cat vs. dog), providing a much richer supervision signal than a binary \"correct\" label.
alt: Bar chart showing probability distribution across three animal classes: Cat at 85 percent, Dog at 10 percent, Fox at 5 percent.
context:
Data selection used the teacher's soft targets as training data (@sec-data-selection-knowledge-distillation-compressing-information-ce68); here they become a compression mechanism. Teacher models transfer semantic knowledge through nonzero probabilities assigned across non-target classes. Whereas a one-hot ground-truth label assigns a probability of one exclusively to the correct class, a teacher's distribution keeps the inter-class correlations known as **dark knowledge**\index{Dark knowledge!definition}, revealing that an input classified as a cat (85 percent) shares subtle semantic features with a dog (10 percent) and a fox (5 percent) (@fig-kd-targets).

[^fn-distillation-etymology-chemistry]: **Distillation**\index{Knowledge distillation!etymology}: The name borrows from the chemical process of separating a mixture. In model compression, the student learns from a teacher's softened output distribution or internal representations rather than copying its parameters. Soft targets can encode relationships among classes, but the student learns only what its objective and training data expose. The metaphor is useful but not literal, since the temperature parameter comes from softmax scaling, and the size-quality trade-off depends on the student, data, objective, and training procedure [@hinton2015distilling]. Deployment savings come from the student architecture, not from the metaphor itself.

title: Knowledge Distillation Workflow
caption: **Knowledge Distillation Workflow**: An input sample passes through both the teacher and the student network. The teacher produces soft labels via temperature-scaled softmax, while the student output is compared against both the soft labels (distillation loss) and the hard labels (student loss).
alt: Block diagram showing knowledge distillation. Input flows to both teacher and student models. Teacher outputs soft labels via temperature-scaled softmax. Student outputs feed into distillation loss and student loss functions.
context:
:::

Training a student model requires balancing teacher imitation against ground-truth task supervision. Operationally, the workflow requires four decisions before training begins: selecting a teacher with the desired behavior, designing a student whose dense architecture satisfies the target accelerator's memory and compute budget, generating soft targets over the training corpus, and choosing the temperature and loss weights that govern optimization. In the resulting dual-path pipeline, an input sample $\ModelInput$ passes through both the teacher and the student, temperature-scaled soft predictions ($\DistillationTemperature > 1$) feed the distillation loss, and unscaled student predictions ($\DistillationTemperature = 1$) are scored against ground-truth hard labels (@fig-kd-overview).

title: Neural Architecture Search Flow
caption: **Neural Architecture Search Flow**: An automated optimization loop for architecture discovery. The search strategy samples candidate subnetworks from a predefined search space, while the performance estimation engine evaluates candidates against target accuracy and hardware constraints (such as latency or energy), feeding reward signals back to steer subsequent exploration toward Pareto-optimal designs.
alt: Three-box flowchart showing NAS process. Search Space box feeds into Search Strategy box, which exchanges architecture and performance estimate with Performance Estimation Strategy box in a feedback loop.
context:
Discovery runs as a closed loop. The search strategy samples candidate architectures $\CandidateArchitecture\in \ArchitectureSearchSpace$ from the defined search space, and the performance estimation engine evaluates their latency or accuracy and feeds the result back to refine subsequent proposals (@fig-nas-flow). NAS[^fn-nas-hardware-aware] returns graphs that sit on the Pareto frontier under explicit resource bounds.

[^fn-nas-hardware-aware]: **Hardware-aware NAS**\index{NAS!hardware-aware}: Optimizes measured latency rather than FLOPs, which can diverge by 3--5$\times$ when memory access or operator support dominates. @tan2019 fed device latency into search and found architectures 1.8$\times$ faster than MobileNetV2 at higher accuracy.

title: Early Exit Architecture
caption: **Early Exit Architecture**: Transformer layers dynamically adjust computation by classifying each layer's output and enabling early termination if sufficient confidence is reached, reducing average latency and power when many inputs can exit before the final layer. Source: [@xin2021].
alt: Flowchart with input feeding transformer layers 1 through N sub L in sequence. Each layer connects to a classifier, confidence estimator, and exit point. Arrows show continue paths for low confidence.

title: Switch Transformer Architecture
caption: **Switch Transformer Architecture**: Replacing dense feedforward layers with a Switching FFN layer (left) enables sparse conditional routing. A gating network routes each token to a single expert (right) out of a large pool, decoupling total model capacity (parameters) from per-token compute cost (FLOPs). Source: [@fedus2022switch].
alt: Two-part diagram. Left shows switch transformer block with self-attention, add-normalize, switching FFN layer, and add-normalize. Right shows expanded view with router selecting one of four FFN experts per token based on probability.
context:
Sparse activation trades compute for memory. A token routed to one of $\ExpertCount$ experts executes arithmetic against only $1/\ExpertCount$ of the expert parameters, yet an all-resident deployment keeps all $\ExpertCount$ expert matrices in device memory. At low batch sizes, divergent routing also leaves each expert with too few tokens to keep matrix units busy, and uneven token distribution overloads some experts while others sit idle.

In a Switch Transformer block, a Switching FFN layer sits inside the standard transformer stack, and its gating router dispatches individual tokens ("More" with $\RouterGateProbability=0.65$, "Parameters" with $\RouterGateProbability=0.8$) to distinct expert sub-blocks (FFN 2 and FFN 1) while unselected experts stay idle (@fig-switch-transformer).

title: Illustrative Quantization Regimes
caption: **Illustrative Quantization Regimes**: The curves depict a qualitative plateau followed by an accuracy cliff as bit width falls. Their breakpoints are illustrative; actual boundaries depend on the model, layer distributions, quantizer, calibration or training method, and evaluation task.
alt: Illustrative line chart of accuracy versus precision. Two example curves remain nearly flat over part of the range and then fall at different low-bit thresholds. Shaded regions mark a low-loss plateau and a model-dependent cliff.
section: Numerical Precision: Changing How Values Are Stored {#sec-model-compression-quantization-precision-cd46}
context:
The accuracy cost varies by model, task, quantizer, calibration data, and bit width. Many convolutional neural network (CNN) inference models tolerate INT8 well; transformers, speech models, and outlier-heavy layers may need different granularity, mixed precision, or training-aware methods. The main approaches are **post-training quantization**\index{Post-training quantization!overview} (PTQ), **quantization-aware training**\index{Quantization-aware training!definition} (QAT), and mixed-precision or **extreme quantization**\index{Quantization!extreme (INT4, binary)} for lower-bit deployment. They differ in training cost and control, not in a guaranteed ordering of accuracy.

The viability of each approach depends on how much precision a given model architecture can shed before quality degrades. Across precision formats from FP32 down to INT2, both CNN and transformer curves exhibit a low-loss plateau where INT8 quantization closely matches full-precision performance, followed by a steep accuracy cliff at lower bit widths where representational capacity breaks down. Because tolerable accuracy degradation depends on end-to-end application constraints, engineering teams must evaluate these cliff boundaries for each target workload and range-calibration recipe (@fig-quantization-free-lunch).

title: Floating-Point Bit Layouts
caption: **Floating-Point Bit Layouts**: Bit allocation trades dynamic range against significand precision. FP32 uses 8 exponent and 23 fraction bits. BF16 retains FP32's 8-bit exponent and therefore a similar numerical range, but reduces the fraction to 7 bits. FP16 uses 5 exponent and 10 fraction bits, providing more significand precision than BF16 but a narrower range that can require loss scaling during training.
alt: Three horizontal bit-layout diagrams. FP32 shows 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, and 23 fraction bits. FP16 shows 1 sign bit, 5 exponent bits, and 10 fraction bits. BF16 shows 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, and 7 fraction bits.
context:
: **Numerical Precision Formats**: Storage ratios reflect raw value width; compute speed and power effects depend on hardware support and workload behavior. {#tbl-numerics tbl-colwidths="[15,12,13,18,18,24]"}

At 16 bits, FP16 and BF16 halve memory storage relative to FP32 while targeting dedicated matrix execution units (such as NVIDIA Tensor Cores and Google TPUs) to accelerate arithmetic throughput. The range-versus-precision trade between them is established with mixed-precision training in @sec-model-training-mixedprecision-training-9218, and @fig-3float shows the bit layouts that set it. BF16 keeps FP32's 8-bit exponent and therefore its dynamic range, whereas FP16 spends more bits on the fraction and caps finite values at 65,504, which is why FP16 training needs loss scaling and BF16 training does not. For inference, the same range limits decide whether activations with large outliers survive the narrower format. TensorFloat-32 (TF32) adopts a hybrid compromise. It retains the 8-bit exponent of FP32 and the 10-bit fraction of FP16, executing on Tensor Cores to accelerate matrix multiplication while storing values in standard 32-bit memory.

title: Quantization Engineering Workflow
caption: **Quantization Engineering Workflow**: The tiers order deployment paths by engineering and validation effort, not by format or guaranteed accuracy. PTQ serves as the initial candidate because it operates over frozen weights with zero retraining cost; QAT introduces simulated quantization into the training loop when quality recovery demands backpropagation; specialized sub-4-bit and binary formats require custom kernel execution and extensive hardware-specific validation. Representation choices such as INT8 versus INT4, per-channel scaling, and mixed precision apply across these stages rather than defining separate maturity levels.
alt: Tiered diagram with three levels ordered by engineering effort: post-training calibration without retraining, quantization-aware retraining for accuracy recovery, and specialized sub-4-bit formats requiring custom execution support.
context:
Reducing numerical bit width relieves memory traffic and arithmetic energy, but naive truncation introduces quantization noise that degrades model accuracy. Deploying low-precision representations requires structured strategies that control where and how bit widths change across the computational graph.

Post-training quantization, quantization-aware training, and extreme low-bit formats differ chiefly in the training and validation cost they require. Representation choices, such as selecting INT8 versus INT4, mixing bit widths across sensitive layers, or choosing per-tensor versus per-channel ranges, are orthogonal options evaluated *within* these workflows rather than separate maturity levels. Ordered by the engineering effort each requires, the deployment sequence moves from fast post-training range calibration through quantization-aware retraining to custom low-bit pipelines (@fig-quantization-roadmap).

title: Illustrative Aggregate Quantization Residuals
caption: **Illustrative Aggregate Quantization Residuals**: Illustrative aggregate residual distribution across heterogeneous scales and clipped values. Within one unclipped uniform quantizer, rounding error is bounded by $[-\QuantizationScale/2, \QuantizationScale/2]$ for step size $\QuantizationScale$; the displayed tails represent clipping or aggregation across different step sizes.
alt: Illustrative histogram of aggregate quantization residuals centered near zero, with tails representing clipping or aggregation across values that use different quantization step sizes.
context:
:::

Rounding to a uniform grid introduces an error with a precise bound. A uniform quantizer maps each value to the nearest of evenly spaced levels separated by a step size $\QuantizationScale$ (range calibration derives $\QuantizationScale$ from the tensor's clipping range in @eq-quant-scale, later in this section). For any value inside the clipping range, rounding to the nearest level misses by at most half a step, so within-range error is bounded by $[-\QuantizationScale/2, \QuantizationScale/2]$. Aggregated across many tensors, most error concentrates inside that bound, while the tails carry the larger distortion that comes from saturation clipping and from mixing tensors that use different step sizes (@fig-quantization-error-dist). Many CNNs tolerate INT8 well, whereas large transformers often need outlier-aware or mixed-precision schemes because a few activation channels carry extreme values. Selecting the appropriate numerical precision therefore requires balancing accuracy constraints, hardware support, and efficiency gains.

title: Post-Training Quantization Pipeline
caption: **Post-Training Quantization Pipeline**: PTQ converts a trained FP32 model directly to INT8 without retraining. Representative calibration data passes through the model to record activation ranges $[\ClippingRangeLowerBound, \ClippingRangeUpperBound]$, computing scale factor $\QuantizationScale$ and zero-point $\QuantizationZeroPoint$ parameters to quantize parameters before deployment.
alt: Vertical flowchart with four boxes connected by arrows. Pretrained model and calibration data feed into calibration step, which feeds into quantization step, producing final quantized model output.

title: Activation Distribution
caption: **Activation Distribution**: ResNet-50 layer activations exhibit a long tail, with outlier values that can lead to inefficient precision use if not handled carefully. Source: [@wu2020integer].
alt: Histogram of ResNet50 activation values showing right-skewed distribution. Most values cluster near zero with long tail extending to outliers around 2.1.
context:
The single calibration pass over $\CalibrationDataset$ avoids retraining, and FP32-to-INT8 weight quantization cuts raw stored weight values by 4$\times$ before scale, zero-point, and packing metadata. The price is that the static activation ranges fixed in the loop risk saturation or wasted integer levels when the calibration data misses deployment tails. The quantization step then converts model parameters to the lower-precision format, producing the final quantized model.

Mapping an unnecessarily wide real-valued interval to the 256 discrete bins of an 8-bit integer wastes numerical resolution on empty range, whereas clipping too aggressively truncates signal. Three calibration methods balance this clipping-versus-resolution trade-off: **max**\index{Quantization calibration!max method} sets bounds to the absolute extremum (preserving extreme values at the cost of vulnerability to outliers), **entropy**\index{Quantization calibration!entropy method} selects bounds by minimizing the Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence between original and quantized distributions, and **percentile**\index{Quantization calibration!percentile method} retains a chosen fraction (such as 99.9 percent) and clips the remaining tail. In one ResNet-50 layer, the dense bulk of activations clusters below 1.1, while a sparse outlier tail stretching past 2.0 motivates testing a candidate clipping boundary near 1.1 to allocate more INT8 bins to the bulk (@fig-resnet-activations-histogram). Choosing a percentile boundary requires cumulative activation counts; the illustrated boundary is not assigned a percentile rank. Task validation must establish whether clipping that tail preserves important rare cases.

title: Calibration Range Selection
caption: **Calibration Range Selection**: Symmetric vs. asymmetric affine quantization mappings. Symmetric quantization (left) forces real zero to map to integer zero, using equal-magnitude negative and positive clipping bounds at the expense of wasted dynamic range for skewed activation distributions; asymmetric quantization (right) uses an explicit zero-point offset $\QuantizationZeroPoint$ to map non-centered ranges $[\ClippingRangeLowerBound, \ClippingRangeUpperBound]$ efficiently.
alt: Two side-by-side mapping diagrams. Left shows symmetric calibration with range from -1 to 1 mapping to -127 to 127 with zero aligned. Right shows asymmetric calibration with range -0.5 to 1.5 mapping to -128 to 127 with a shifted zero point.
context:
##### Tuning quantization ranges {#sec-model-compression-tuning-quantization-ranges-439d}

Once calibration identifies clipping boundaries $[\ClippingRangeLowerBound, \ClippingRangeUpperBound]$, the range must be mapped onto integer endpoints, and two mapping schemes dominate (@fig-calibration-ranges). A **symmetric**\index{Quantization!symmetric} mapping uses a zero-centered range with zero-point zero, forcing real zero to integer zero by mapping $[-1, 1]$ directly onto $[-127, 127]$. An **asymmetric**\index{Quantization!asymmetric} mapping keeps one scale but a generally nonzero zero-point $\QuantizationZeroPoint$, which accommodates skewed activation intervals such as $[-0.5, 1.5]$ across $[-128, 127]$.

title: Quantization Range Variation
caption: **Quantization Range Variation**: Different convolutional filters can have different weight ranges, motivating per-filter quantization to reduce quantization error. The differing clipping scales illustrate the choice between one layerwise range and separate channelwise ranges. Source: [@gholami2022].
alt: Four rows showing CNN filters with Gaussian weight distributions. Each filter has different clipping ranges shown as red and blue dashed lines. Layer-wise clipping uses same range; channel-wise uses per-filter ranges.
context:
Quantization granularity governs how broadly scale factors and zero-points are shared across a tensor, balancing representation resolution against metadata overhead and execution complexity. In convolutional filters or transformer projection matrices, weight magnitudes often vary widely across individual channels. Sharing a single scale factor across an entire tensor risks collapsing the dynamic range of small-magnitude channels to zero; conversely, assigning scales per channel preserves local variance at the expense of tracking additional scale vectors during matrix multiplication.

When weight channels exhibit divergent standard deviations, sharing a single clipping threshold across an entire layer either collapses small-magnitude channels or clips wider channels. Across convolutional channels (filters 1 through $\LayerOutputWidth$), a global layerwise threshold spans the widest distribution at the cost of resolution in narrower filters, whereas per-channel clipping boundaries adapt tightly to each filter's dynamic range (@fig-quantization-granularity).

title: Quantized Matrix Multiplication Pipeline
caption: **Quantized Matrix Multiplication Pipeline**: Floating-point weights and activation inputs are quantized to INT8 (violet), fed into integer SIMD/Tensor Core matrix multiplication (blue), accumulated in 32-bit registers (red), and requantized back to INT8 (green) before non-linear activation. From the HarvardX TinyML course.
alt: Matrix multiplication diagram. Violet boxes quantize floating-point inputs to INT8 before matrix multiplication, a blue block performs the multiplication, a red box shows the INT32 intermediate output, a green block requantizes before activation, and a green box shows the final INT8 output.

title: Quantization-Aware Training Pipeline
caption: **Quantization-Aware Training Pipeline**: QAT inserts fake-quantization nodes into the forward graph to simulate low-precision clipping and rounding errors during training. Backpropagation updates floating-point master weights using straight-through estimators (STE), allowing network parameters to adapt to numerical noise before exporting fixed integer scales for inference.
alt: Vertical flowchart showing QAT process. Pretrained model feeds into quantization step, then retraining/fine-tuning step with training data input, producing final quantized model output.
context:
#### Quantization-aware training {#sec-model-compression-quantizationaware-training-4032}

Quantization-aware training incorporates numerical rounding noise directly into the optimization graph. A pretrained model is quantized and then retrained or fine-tuned on the training dataset, which yields a low-precision model whose parameters have adapted to rounding noise (@fig-qat).

title: PTQ-to-QAT Pipeline
caption: **PTQ-to-QAT Pipeline**: PTQ calibration can initialize ranges and scales before QAT fine-tunes the pretrained weights with simulated quantization. Calibration data feeds the PTQ stage, and training data feeds QAT.
alt: Vertical flowchart with two grouped stages. PTQ stage shows pretrained model through quantize and calibrate steps. QAT stage shows fine-tuning step. Calibrate data feeds PTQ; training data feeds QAT.
context:
:::

Rather than training from scratch or cold-starting scale parameters, production workflows frequently initialize QAT using scale factors derived during an initial PTQ calibration pass. In this two-phase pipeline, a PTQ phase feeds calibration data into the pretrained model to establish initial scale metadata, and the resulting PTQ checkpoint enters a QAT phase in which the full training data drives fine-tuning (@fig-ptq-qat).

title: Illustrative Quantization Scenario
caption: **Illustrative Quantization Scenario**: Paired bars separate FP32 and INT8 alternatives. The right panel shows illustrative weight storage, where reducing each weight from 32 to 8 bits produces an exact fourfold decrease; the left panel shows illustrative, architecture-dependent latency changes.
alt: Two paired bar charts compare FP32 and INT8. The left chart shows illustrative inference time in milliseconds for Inception v3, MobileNet v1, and ResNet v2. The right chart shows raw weight storage in megabytes, with every INT8 bar one quarter the FP32 bar.
context:
:::

Across three vision networks (Inception v3, MobileNet v1, and ResNet v2), INT8 conversion contracts weight storage by exactly $4\times$ (135 MB to 33.75 MB for the illustrative Inception bar), while the latency change varies with the architecture and its kernels (@fig-quantization-impact).

title: Block Sparse Representation
caption: **Block Sparse Representation**: Grouping non-zero weights into dense sub-blocks and storing an auxiliary index array lets matching kernels skip empty blocks. The $3\times3$ tiles illustrate the representation; efficient GPU execution depends on supported block shapes, layouts, and kernels. Adapted from NVIDIA cuSPARSE documentation [@nvidia_cusparse_block].
alt: Grid of 3×3 matrix blocks with varying shades indicating dense submatrices. Adjacent index array shows non zero block positions. Gray blocks represent zeros, colored blocks represent dense submatrices stored separately.
context:
Structured patterns resolve the break-even problem by constraining where zeros occur, and achieving actual speedups from them requires hardware that can efficiently skip zero-valued computations. Processor architectures differ in which patterns they exploit. Ampere-generation and later Sparse Tensor Cores exploit fine-grained 2:4 structured patterns, while systolic arrays require dense block structures. Libraries such as cuSPARSE reformulate sparse computations into patterns the hardware handles well, and MegaBlocks [@gale2022megablocksefficientsparsetraining] recasts sparse mixture-of-experts training as block-sparse operations on dense tiles.

A sparse pattern earns hardware speedup only when it is regular enough for kernels to predict. Two formats make that regularity explicit: block sparse matrices and N:M sparsity patterns. Block sparse matrices group nonzeros into dense submatrices, so operations on the large sparse matrix become a smaller number of dense operations on submatrices. In the illustrated representation, $3\times 3$ dense sub-blocks are indexed by an auxiliary coordinate array, so sub-block kernels can bypass the empty tiles (@fig-block-sparse-gemm) [@nvidia_cusparse_block]. The block size is a teaching choice. Actual speedup requires a block shape, layout, datatype, and kernel supported by the target library and hardware; regular blocks alone do not guarantee aligned memory transactions or Tensor Core execution.

title: Compression Methods in One Reported Setting
caption: **Compression Methods in One Reported Setting**: The cited comparison plots accuracy change against model-size ratio for pruning, quantization, their combination, and SVD. In this setting, pruning plus quantization reaches the smallest ratio near baseline accuracy; the ordering is model- and implementation-specific. Source: [@han2016deep].
alt: Line graph of accuracy change versus model-size ratio with four series for pruning plus quantization, pruning, quantization, and SVD. The combined method reaches the smallest size near baseline accuracy in this reported setting.
context:
Sequencing matters because these transformations interact through shared parameters and activation distributions. Structural pruning removes channels or attention heads, altering the dynamic range and variance of surviving weight tensors. Quantizing before pruning can leave ranges poorly matched to the resulting distributions, so recalibration or joint adaptation may be needed. In the staged candidate, floating-point recovery lets the pruned network adapt, and distillation supplies a teacher signal before final quantization. QAT itself updates floating-point master weights through approximate gradients; it does not require direct integer weight updates. Alternative schedules should be compared at matched recovery and calibration budgets.

Combining techniques also changes the size-quality trade-off itself [@han2016deep]. In one reported setting (@fig-compression-methods), while individual SVD and pruning curves suffer steep accuracy cliffs below about 15 percent and 6 percent model size respectively, combining pruning with quantization extends the zero-loss plateau down to roughly 3 percent of original parameter footprint. This comparison does not isolate transformation order. The magnitude of these gains remains model- and runtime-specific, requiring engineers to validate each transformation stage independently.

title: First-Layer Convolutional Filter Patterns
caption: **First-Layer Convolutional Filter Patterns**: An $8\times5$ grid groups stylized kernels into edge, color, frequency, mixed, and uniform-looking patterns. Appearance alone does not establish inactivity; pruning requires measured activation or importance evidence in addition to low weight variance.
alt: Grid of 40 stylized first-layer convolutional filters, arranged in eight columns and five rows. The final row appears nearly uniform but is labeled as requiring activation evidence rather than being classified as inactive from appearance alone.
context:
Diagnostic inspection verifies numerical integrity, the step that remains after framework APIs create and calibrate the compressed model and hardware optimization libraries lower it to the execution substrate (@sec-model-compression-implementation-tools-4990). While system-scale validation and artifact monitoring belong to downstream deployment infrastructure, the immediate diagnostic task is verifying that quantization clipping, pruning masks, or sparsity patterns have not perturbed internal feature distributions beyond acceptable task error tolerances.

Quantization error histograms show whether error is broadly distributed or concentrated in outliers. Activation visualizations help detect clipping, overflow, and saturation. In a grid of first-layer convolutional filters, the top rows show distinct edge, color, and frequency detectors, while the bottom row shows uniform-looking filters that appear redundant at a glance but require measured activation tracing before they can be pruned safely (@fig-color-mapping). Framework observers and debuggers can expose quantization ranges and tensor error, while compiler or runtime inspectors can show the graph and kernels that the exported model actually executes.

title: Anatomy of a Modern AI Accelerator
caption: **Anatomy of a Modern AI Accelerator**: This generic schematic combines common components rather than depicting one product. A host interface connects the accelerator to a CPU, a high-bandwidth device-memory interface feeds shared on-chip storage, and processing elements contain matrix, vector, and special-function units with local memory. Real accelerators differ in which units they provide and whether storage is hardware-managed cache or software-managed scratchpad.
alt: Generic schematic of an AI accelerator chip linked by a host interface to a host CPU and by a memory interface to high-bandwidth memory. Inside the chip, rows of processing elements surround shared on-chip storage. An enlarged processing element contains an L1 cache or scratchpad, a tensor core, a vector unit, and a special function unit (SFU). A separate dashed link connects host DRAM to the host CPU.
context:
The anatomy of an accelerator\index{Accelerator!anatomy} is the arrangement of parts that every machine learning accelerator shares: arithmetic units built for tensor operations, on-chip memory that holds operands next to those units, a wide path to off-chip memory, and a host interface through which work arrives. Every inference and every training step on such a machine is a stream of operand movements that ends in multiply-accumulate operations, and the anatomy decides how far each operand travels before it is used. A matrix unit that can retire thousands of multiply-accumulates per cycle sits idle whenever its next operands are still in flight, and an off-chip access can take many processor cycles and cost orders of magnitude more energy than the low-precision operation it feeds. The arithmetic units are the easy part of the design; the rest of the anatomy exists to keep them fed.

The definition becomes concrete in the generic chip of @fig-accelerator-anatomy, which serves as this chapter's map. External high-bandwidth memory (HBM) feeds shared on-chip storage (an L2 cache), which distributes operands into rows of processing elements\index{Processing element!accelerator building block}, each equipped with a private scratchpad or cache, a matrix unit, a vector unit, and a special function unit. A host interface connects the chip to the CPU that issues its work.

title: The Iron Law Heatmap
caption: **The Iron Law Heatmap**: Total system speedup as a function of accelerator gain ($\AcceleratorGain$) and accelerated fraction ($\ParallelFraction$). High speedup appears only near the top-right corner, where both accelerator gain and accelerated fraction are high. At $\ParallelFraction=0.9$, for example, even an infinite gain on the accelerated path cannot exceed 10$\times$ end-to-end speedup. Contours span roughly 1$\times$–200$\times$ speedup.
alt: Heatmap of speedup vs. accelerator gain and accelerated fraction. High speedup in red and orange appears near the top-right corner where the accelerated fraction is near 1.0 and accelerator gain is high; lower-fraction regions remain blue. White contour lines labeled 2x to 50x follow the lower bands, a colorbar at the right labels every band from 1x to 500x, and text labels mark a High Accelerated Fraction region above and an Unaccelerated Bound region below.
context:
[^fn-amdahls-law-acceleration]: **Amdahl's law**\index{Amdahl's law!acceleration ceiling}: Maps onto the iron law only after the proposed change is specified. If a faster tensor unit reduces the computation term $(\Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw))$ but leaves data transfer and fixed latency unchanged, those unaffected terms bound total speedup. A different accelerator or memory system may improve bandwidth as well. The unaccelerated fraction is therefore defined by the intervention, not by a permanent classification of each term as serial.

This dynamic explains why hardware upgrades frequently fail to produce proportional end-to-end speedups. @Fig-iron-law-heatmap maps system speedup across accelerator gain ($\AcceleratorGain$) and accelerated fraction ($\ParallelFraction$), charting where those returns diminish\index{Amdahl's law!diminishing returns}. Where the unaccelerated fraction $1-\ParallelFraction$ remains substantial, the white contour curves flatten horizontally into the unaccelerated-bound regime, bounding total speedup at the $1/(1-\ParallelFraction)$ asymptote regardless of how far $\AcceleratorGain$ scales along the horizontal axis.

title: Hardware Specialization Timeline
caption: **Hardware Specialization Timeline**: Computing architectures evolve through recurring cycles of specialization and integration across five eras. Each era introduces domain-specific hardware to resolve an important memory or arithmetic bottleneck, from off-chip FPUs to GPUs, codecs, and TPU/Tensor Core array units. Many of these capabilities later appear alongside CPUs in broader systems, even when the specialized units remain distinct.
alt: Five-column timeline from the 1980s through the 2020s. The columns list floating-point and signal processing (Intel 8087, TMS32010 DSP), 3D graphics and multimedia (early GPUs, GeForce 256), real-time media and network processing (H.264 and MP3 codecs, IXP2800), deep-learning tensor operations (Google TPU v1 and NVIDIA Tensor Cores), and application-specific acceleration (AI engines, SmartNICs, and multi-chip and wafer-scale systems).
context:
The payoff arrived in 2012, when AlexNet\index{AlexNet!GPU deep learning era} [@krizhevsky2012imagenet] won the ImageNet competition after training on two consumer GPUs, the co-design result examined in @sec-introduction-deep-learning-era-infrastructure-bottleneck-2f02. Its dense 2D convolutions mapped directly onto thousands of GPU arithmetic lanes. In D·A·M terms, the machine constraint had dictated which algorithms were feasible, and aligning the algorithm's parallel structure with throughput-oriented hardware lifted it.

Across five eras from the 1980s to the 2020s (@fig-timeline), specialization moved from discrete coprocessors such as the Intel 8087 FPU and TMS32010 DSP through graphics engines and dedicated media codecs to deep-learning tensor arrays and wafer-scale hardware. Each era's specialized unit targets a different bottleneck, yet the principles modern accelerators depend on (dedicating silicon to the dominant operation, staging operands in local memory, and minimizing off-chip data movement) were all in place before deep learning arrived.

title: The Energy Hierarchy
caption: **The Energy Hierarchy**: Representative 45 nm energy estimates on a logarithmic scale from @horowitz2014. An off-chip DRAM access costs about 173$\times$ an FP32 multiply and about 128$\times$ a read from an 8 KB SRAM array in this model; a small, register-adjacent L1 access (about 0.5 pJ in the registry used elsewhere in this chapter) is cheaper still. The values are not universal device specifications; they illustrate why reuse in registers and SRAM can matter more than reducing arithmetic count alone.
alt: Log-scale horizontal bar chart of representative 45-nanometer energy estimates. INT8 addition is 0.03 pJ, FP32 addition is 0.9 pJ, FP32 multiplication is 3.7 pJ, an 8 KB SRAM read is 5 pJ, and a DRAM read is 640 pJ. An arrow from the SRAM bar to the DRAM bar marks an approximately 128-fold difference.
context:
Data access can dominate the energy budget of a memory-intensive kernel.[^fn-von-neumann-bottleneck] On a logarithmic scale, representative 45 nm operation energies span more than four orders of magnitude, from an INT8 addition ($0.03\text{ pJ}$) and an FP32 multiply ($3.7\text{ pJ}$) to an off-chip DRAM fetch ($640\text{ pJ}$) (@fig-energy-hierarchy). This ladder is the chapter's single reference for what moving a value costs; later sections cite it rather than restate it.

[^fn-von-neumann-bottleneck]: **Von Neumann bottleneck**\index{Von Neumann bottleneck!ML accelerator constraint}: Separating storage from compute requires instructions and data to cross interfaces rather than remain in local registers. The exact cost of each crossing changes with technology and operation, but locality remains a first-order design concern.

title: Systolic Array Dataflow Architecture
caption: **Systolic Array Dataflow Architecture**: A pipelined grid of processing elements (PEs) passes operands and partial results between neighbors. The illustrated movement is one possible matrix-multiplication dataflow; designs choose which operand or partial sum remains stationary to match reuse, buffers, and tensor shape. Utilization depends on mapping and dimensions.
alt: Systolic array diagram with a control unit feeding data streams into a processing-element grid. Elements perform multiply-accumulate operations and pass values or partial results to neighboring elements.
context:
Kung\index{Kung, H.T.!systolic array inventor} and Leiserson\index{Leiserson, Charles E.!systolic array inventor}[^fn-systolic-array-dataflow] [@kung1979systolic] first introduced systolic arrays, formalizing their use in parallel computing architectures for efficient matrix operations [@kung1982]. Unlike general-purpose execution units, systolic arrays exploit spatial and temporal locality\index{Data Locality!spatial and temporal} by reusing operands as they propagate through the grid. Google's TPU\index{TPU!systolic array scaling} exemplifies this architectural approach: in the TPUv4, a $128{\times}128$ systolic array\index{Systolic Array!TPU configuration} of multiply-accumulate units\index{Multiply-Accumulate!MAC unit} processes matrix operations by streaming data through the array in a pipelined manner [@jouppi2023]. @Fig-systolic-array traces this 2D pipelined dataflow: a control unit stages operands into input FIFO buffers that stream activation data horizontally across the processing grid, while partial sums accumulate vertically down columns into the bottom adder-accumulator chain. Each processing element performs one multiply-accumulate per cycle and passes its operands to its neighbors, so a value loaded once is reused across an entire row or column rather than refetched from memory.

[^fn-systolic-array-dataflow]: **Systolic array**\index{Systolic Array!dataflow design}: Kung and Leiserson used the term for arrays in which data advances through neighboring processing elements on a regular schedule [@kung1979systolic]. Pipeline fill permits concurrent wavefronts and local reuse. The benefit depends on the stationary operand, tile, buffers, and utilization; it does not guarantee fixed DRAM savings. Irregular workloads and poorly aligned shapes remain a weaker fit because fill, drain, and idle elements consume capacity.

title: 2:4 Structured Sparsity GEMM
caption: **2:4 Structured Sparsity GEMM**: Left: standard dense matrix multiplication on Tensor Cores using full 8-element rows. Right: 2:4 sparse multiplication retains two nonzeros in every group of four and uses compact indices to select matching elements from the dense right-hand matrix. A supported sparse inner loop can halve the multiplied values, although metadata handling and the rest of the execution path determine end-to-end speedup. Source: PyTorch blog [@pytorch_sparsity_blog].
alt: Side-by-side comparison of dense and 2:4 sparse GEMM on Tensor Cores. Left shows an 8-element dense row multiplication. Right shows a sparse row with two retained values per group of four and compact indices selecting matching elements from the dense right-hand matrix.
context:
:::

NVIDIA's Sparse Tensor Cores\index{Sparse Tensor Core!2:4 constraint} implement the 2:4 instance of the N:M pattern\index{Sparsity!structured, 2:4 hardware support} [@NVIDIA2020; @nvidia_cusparse_block]. Their input is the compressed 2:4 encoding, the two retained values of each group plus a 4-bit metadata tag (2 bits per value) recording their original positions. During execution, the memory hierarchy transfers only the compressed weights and their metadata, halving the weight-value payload while adding metadata traffic; total transferred bytes therefore fall by less than half before other overheads. Inside the Sparse Tensor Core datapath, the 4-bit metadata steers an internal multiplexer network that selects the matching two values from an uncompressed four-element activation vector. These selected activations and the two nonzero weights are then routed into a half-sized dot-product multiplier tree. Because the hardware computes only on the nonzeros while streaming compressed weights, this design doubles the peak arithmetic instruction throughput, yielding an advertised 2$\times$ tensor-math speedup over dense operations when weights are fine-tuned to satisfy the pattern (@fig-2-4-gemm).

caption: **Model Size vs. Hardware Bandwidth**: Both series are the base-10 logarithm of growth relative to 2014 (VGG-16 for parameters, one GPU of the dual-GPU K80 board for bandwidth), so each unit on the vertical axis is a tenfold increase. Over the plotted decade dense parameter counts grow roughly `{python} MemoryWallTrend.model_growth_mult_str` against per-device bandwidth's `{python} MemoryWallTrend.bandwidth_growth_mult_str`. The open marker is a sparse expert model plotted at total parameters and excluded from the fit. The shaded band is a gap between logarithms rather than a difference, so its width reads as a ratio, and the fitted trends describe the decade's average rates; the dense frontier has been flat since 2022. Method after @gholami2024.

Red model-size points rise to about 3.5 and blue bandwidth points to about 1.5, with one open red marker for DeepSeek-V3 above the red trend and a gray band shaded between the two trend lines from 2016 onward, labeled in bold as the AI memory wall.
context:
```

Hardware balance is the supply side of the memory wall; model size is the demand side. The structural widening between model footprints and available memory bandwidth is what turns the iron law's memory term into the binding constraint across generations. Parameter count is a capacity quantity. In low-batch dense decoding with weights streamed from device memory, weight traffic per generated token grows with the parameter count. Sparse expert models read selected experts rather than every stored parameter, so their total parameter counts do not directly specify per-token traffic. @Fig-memory-wall plots this logarithmic divergence relative to 2014, contrasting the roughly `{python} MemoryWallTrend.model_growth_mult_str` increase in dense model parameters (filled red points) against the `{python} MemoryWallTrend.bandwidth_growth_mult_str` increase in per-device accelerator memory bandwidth (blue points) to isolate the widening shaded memory-wall gap [@krizhevsky2012imagenet; @simonyan2014very; @brown2020language; @chowdhery2022palm; @dubey2024llama]. DeepSeek-V3 appears as an open marker at its total parameter count and is left out of the trend for exactly that reason [@deepseek2025v3]. Even high-bandwidth accelerators such as NVIDIA B200 and AMD MI300X/MI325X cannot close this growth-rate gap through bandwidth scaling alone [@nvidia2024blackwell; @amd2023mi300x]. Parameter counts for proprietary systems such as GPT-4 and Gemini are not officially disclosed, so they are not plotted as factual data points.

title: Host-Accelerator Data Transfer Sequence
caption: **Host-Accelerator Data Transfer Sequence**: Four-step execution flow between CPU host and GPU device: (1) copying input data over PCIe, (2) issuing kernel instructions, (3) GPU compute, and (4) transferring results back to host memory. Low PCIe bandwidth and host dispatch latencies can easily dominate runtime unless kernel compute time exceeds data transfer overhead.
alt: Four-step data flow diagram: (1) copy data from main memory to GPU memory, (2) CPU instructs GPU, (3) GPU executes in parallel, (4) results copy back to main memory.
context:
In discrete accelerator systems, the host CPU and the accelerator operate as separate computational domains joined by a peripheral bus. The host manages storage I/O, network streams, and runtime orchestration, while the accelerator executes dense mathematical kernels over high-bandwidth device memory. Because CPU memory (system DRAM) and accelerator memory (HBM or GDDR) occupy distinct physical address spaces, computation cannot begin until tensors traverse the host-accelerator interconnect. Host-accelerator data movement\index{Host-Accelerator Communication!transfer bottleneck} therefore establishes an operational boundary: if transfers over the peripheral bus cannot feed the accelerator's compute cores at line rate, the device idles regardless of its raw FLOP/s capacity.

@Fig-host-accelerator-data-movement sequences the four-stage execution trace across host and device lifelines: copying input data across PCIe to device memory via DMA\index{DMA!computation overlap} (step 1), dispatching kernel instructions from the CPU (step 2), executing parallel core compute with local writeback (step 3), and copying results back to host memory (step 4). In a naive synchronous execution model, every transfer step sits directly on the critical path, stalling either the host or the accelerator until each memory transaction finishes.

title: The Rising Ridge
caption: **The Rising Ridge**: Hardware arithmetic intensity (FLOP/byte) over time computed as each chip's dense FP16 tensor peak divided by its memory bandwidth: `{python} RooflineGap.v100_tflop_per_s_str` over `{python} RooflineGap.v100_bw_tb_per_s_str` for V100, `{python} RooflineGap.a100_fp16_tflop_per_s_str` over `{python} RooflineGap.a100_bw_tb_per_s_str` for A100, and `{python} RooflineGap.h100_fp16_tflop_per_s_str` over `{python} RooflineGap.h100_bw_tb_per_s_str` for H100. This is the arithmetic intensity a kernel must reach before compute rather than bandwidth limits it. As compute capability grows faster than memory bandwidth, the ridge point rises from V100 through H100 and remains high on B200. This trend explains why architectures with high data reuse flourish while low-reuse workloads face a growing performance penalty.
alt: Line plot showing dense-FP16 arithmetic intensity ridge points: about 140 FLOP/byte for V100, 153 for A100, 295 for H100, and 281 for B200. Shaded regions indicate memory-rich and compute-dense zones.
context:
Peak computational capability has expanded faster than memory bus performance across accelerator generations, and the size of that mismatch is what sets how much data reuse a kernel needs to stay fed. Across `{python} ComputeBandwidthDivergence.span_str`, NVIDIA's data center generations multiplied dense FP16 compute by `{python} ComputeBandwidthDivergence.compute_growth_mult_str` and memory bandwidth by only `{python} ComputeBandwidthDivergence.bandwidth_growth_mult_str`, a `{python} ComputeBandwidthDivergence.gap_growth_mult_str` rise in the reuse a kernel needs on B200 relative to V100.

That ratio measures how far the hardware ridge point\index{Ridge Point!hardware comparison}, the threshold a kernel must clear to become compute bound, has risen since the V100. @Fig-rising-ridge plots it generation by generation, leaving out the H200 exception, so the doubling of the gap appears directly as the ridge point roughly doubling from V100 (`{python} RooflineGap.v100_ridge_int_str`) to H100 (`{python} RooflineGap.h100_ridge_int_str`) and then holding near that level on B200 (`{python} RooflineGap.b200_ridge_int_str`). A kernel that cleared the V100 ridge comfortably can fall below the H100 ridge without any change to its code, so newer hardware demands more operational reuse before execution reaches peak throughput.

title: Matrix Tiling Mechanics
caption: **Matrix Tiling Mechanics**: Partitioning large matrix multiplication ($\GemmOutputMatrix=\GemmLeftOperand\GemmRightOperand$) into $\GemmTileRowDimension\times \GemmTileInnerDimension$ and $\GemmTileInnerDimension\times \GemmTileColumnDimension$ blocks aligns memory footprints with fast on-chip SRAM/registers. Maximizing register reuse within each tile amortizes slow off-chip DRAM accesses and keeps compute engines operating at peak throughput.
alt: Three matrices A, B, C with highlighted tiles showing how matrix multiplication partitions into smaller blocks. Dimensions labeled M, N, K with corresponding tile sizes Mtile, Ntile, Ktile.
context:
[^fn-tiling-cache-reuse]: **Tiling (loop blocking)**\index{Tiling!DRAM traffic reduction}: This restructuring partitions a computation into blocks sized for a fast local tier. A naive loop makes repeated references to the same elements; caches may capture some, while blocking deliberately concentrates reuse before eviction [@lam1991]. This reduction in lower-tier traffic is a primary source of the gap between naive matrix multiplication and optimized GEMM routines.

The naïve loop nest of @lst-matmul_data_movement shows the cost of leaving reuse to chance. Written as $\GemmOutputMatrix= \GemmLeftOperand\GemmRightOperand$, with the weights as $\GemmLeftOperand$ and the input batch as $\GemmRightOperand$, it references the same elements of both operands again and again, and without tiling those repeated accesses consume unnecessary bandwidth. Some references can hit in cache, but large matrices and an unfavorable traversal order can still cause excessive lower-tier traffic. Tiling partitions this multiplication across its three principal dimensions ($\GemmRowDimension$, $\GemmInnerDimension$, and $\GemmColumnDimension$) (@fig-tiling-diagram). Each highlighted region represents the working set staged in fast memory at one moment: an $\GemmTileRowDimension{\times}\GemmTileInnerDimension$ block of $\GemmLeftOperand$ (within the green row band) multiplies a $\GemmTileInnerDimension{\times}\GemmTileColumnDimension$ block of $\GemmRightOperand$ (within the pink column band) to accumulate one $\GemmTileRowDimension{\times}\GemmTileColumnDimension$ output tile ($\text{Block}_{\TileRowIndex,n}$, shaded blue) of $\GemmOutputMatrix$. Processing all inner-product operations for an active tile before evicting it amortizes off-chip DRAM latency across $\GemmTileRowDimension\cdot \GemmTileColumnDimension\cdot \GemmTileInnerDimension$ arithmetic operations.

title: Benchmark Workflow Components
caption: **Benchmark Workflow Components**: Read left to right: each stage fixes assumptions for the next, carrying an audio anomaly-detection task from problem definition to a reproducible embedded-device benchmark run. Values from @banbury2021mlperftiny.
alt: Nine-stage workflow labeled Problem definition, Dataset selection (public domain), Model selection, Model training code, Derive Tiny version: Quantization, Embedded implementation, Benchmarking harness integration, Deploy on device, and Example benchmark run, with an audio anomaly-detection implementation diagram below.
context:
### A complete reference benchmark {#sec-benchmarking-example-benchmark-229f}

MLPerf Tiny's anomaly-detection benchmark shows every component fixed at once on one small embedded model. The multi-stage pipeline in @fig-benchmark-components traces this industrial audio benchmark across nine sequential phases, carrying the task from problem definition in the top chevrons through spectrogram extraction, autoencoder training, and INT8 quantization down to embedded deployment on an ARM mbed OS microcontroller. Each stage fixes boundary conditions for the next: the problem definition dictates the acoustic sampling rate and input representation (Data); the dataset properties and task objective determine feasible model architectures (Algorithm); and the microcontroller's hardware limits (SRAM capacity, energy envelope, and real-time latency deadlines) dictate INT8 quantization and memory-efficient kernel compilation (Machine). Here every choice constrains the next, so a benchmark that measures only classification accuracy or only raw inference latency misses cross-stage interactions, where an engineering decision at any stage narrows the feasible design space downstream.

title: Benchmarking Granularity
caption: **Benchmarking Granularity**: Four-panel block diagram showing micro, macro, application, and end-to-end evaluation layers. Each panel maps a distinct scope of assessment, from isolated kernel operations through full-system deployment, enabling targeted optimization at every level of the ML stack.
alt: Block diagram showing four evaluation layers: micro (kernels), macro (models), application (compute logic), and end-to-end (full deployment), linked by dashed lines to show expanding scope.
section: │ Goal: Component-only vs end-to-end speedup under pipeline overhead.
context:
Optimization techniques operate across distinct granularities: kernel fusion targets micro-level execution, structured pruning alters macro-level parameter structures, and data curation\index{Data curation!end-to-end generalization} determines end-to-end generalization. System validation must align with these respective boundaries. An isolated micro-benchmark may show substantial kernel speedup, yet a macro-benchmark can reveal that increased activation memory footprints force smaller batch sizes that degrade overall throughput. Similarly, an end-to-end benchmark exposes storage or host deserialization stalls that remain completely invisible at the accelerator kernel level.

Measurement perimeters widen from left to right in @fig-granularity, and the figure inserts one tier between macro and end-to-end. Micro-benchmarks isolate kernel layers (ML Layers) and macro-benchmarks evaluate composed models (ML Model). An application benchmark then adds the supporting host compute around the model (AI Task), and the end-to-end benchmark adds the non-AI compute nodes the request also traverses. The three granularities in this section fold the application tier into end-to-end, but the four-tier view shows where bottlenecks migrate as the boundary widens: out of the accelerator and into the host systems around it.

title: Isolation vs. Representativeness
caption: **Isolation vs. Representativeness**: The core trade-off in benchmarking granularity. Micro-benchmarks provide high diagnostic precision but limited real-world relevance, while end-to-end benchmarks capture realistic system behavior but offer less precise component-level insights. Effective ML system evaluation requires strategic combination of all three levels.
alt: Scatter plot with three labeled points along a diagonal: micro-benchmarks at high isolation, macro-benchmarks, and end-to-end benchmarks at high representativeness.
context:
```

Selecting a single granularity level is rarely sufficient because benchmarking presents an inherent trade-off between diagnostic isolation and production fidelity. Along the descending diagonal in @fig-benchmark-tradeoffs, evaluation regimes trade diagnostic power for operational realism: micro-benchmarks (the red point at the top left) isolate kernel-level memory bandwidth and warp occupancy at the expense of end-to-end context, macro-benchmarks (the blue center point) capture composed model topologies, and end-to-end benchmarks (the green point at the bottom right) encompass live production traffic but obscure the root causes of latency spikes. Effective evaluation requires strategically combining all three tiers to verify that kernel speedups survive full-system deployment.

title: ImageNet Error and GPU Adoption
caption: **ImageNet Error and GPU Adoption**: Sourced top-5 error rates are shown beside GPU use among challenge entries. The temporal association does not isolate hardware's causal contribution. Error-rate sources: [@russakovsky2015; @krizhevsky2012imagenet]. @gray2015ilsvrcgpu charts the per-year GPU entry counts.
alt: Dual-axis chart with a blue line showing top-5 error rate declining and green bars showing increased GPU use among ImageNet challenge entries from 2010 to 2014.
context:
:::

System benchmarks evaluate performance across scales, ranging from single-chip configurations to large distributed systems and covering both training and inference. The ImageNet challenge shows why separating the hardware's contribution from the model's is hard to do after the fact. Between 2010 and 2014, top-5 error (the blue line in @fig-imagenet-gpus) fell from 28.2 percent to 7.3 percent while GPU-accelerated entries (the green bars) rose from zero to over 100, with the steepest single drop at AlexNet's arrival in 2012 [@krizhevsky2012imagenet; @russakovsky2015; @gray2015ilsvrcgpu]. These paired series plot contemporaneous empirical trends, not a causal attribution of how much accuracy gain stemmed from hardware throughput versus algorithmic design, training schedules, or dataset expansion. A system benchmark avoids that ambiguity by construction: it fixes the model and quality target so that any change in the result belongs to the hardware-software stack.

title: MLPerf Training Progress

### Training benchmark motivation {#sec-benchmarking-training-benchmark-motivation-f365}

MLPerf Training\index{MLPerf Training!standardized framework} [@mattson2020mlperf; @mlperf_training_website] provides the standardized framework for this time-to-quality measurement. title: Power Consumption Differentials
caption: **Power Consumption Differentials**: Measured power spans about eight orders of magnitude across MLPerf divisions, from milliwatts for TinyML submissions through watts at the edge to kilowatts in data center inference and hundreds of kilowatts for training systems. Each pair marks the lowest and highest power among official MLPerf Power submissions in that division, after @tschand2025.

context:
:::

Measuring power differs fundamentally from measuring execution time. Latency is a single interval, but instantaneous power (supply voltage times current) fluctuates continuously across microsecond execution phases and drifts over minutes as silicon heats up, increasing temperature-dependent leakage current. ML deployments also span an extreme physical range. The dumbbell plot in @fig-power-differentials isolates this disparity on a logarithmic power scale, plotting minimum (blue) and maximum (red) envelopes across four deployment tiers: TinyML systems (5.6 mW to 167 mW), edge hardware (3.9 W to 1.1 kW), data center inference nodes (267 W to 6.3 kW), and large-scale training clusters (5.5 kW to 498 kW). Spanning about eight orders of magnitude from the TinyML floor to the training-cluster ceiling, this spectrum explains why no single efficiency metric serves all deployment contexts. A figure of merit optimized for multi-rack data center throughput becomes meaningless for a battery-powered keyword spotter governed by milliwatt budgets.

title: Power Measurement Boundaries
caption: **Power Measurement Boundaries**: MLPerf defines system boundaries for power measurement, ranging from single-chip devices to full data center nodes, to enable fair comparisons of energy efficiency across diverse hardware platforms. context:
### Power measurement boundaries {#sec-benchmarking-power-measurement-boundaries-982c}

Where an engineer draws the system boundary dictates what counts as efficient. If a benchmark measures only the accelerator core, it ignores the host CPU driving the PCIe bus, the off-chip DRAM holding weights, and the cooling fans dissipating heat. @Fig-power-diagram partitions these measurement perimeters across three deployment tiers (Tiny, Inference, and Training), where solid olive enclosures demarcate measured components and red dashed boxes isolate excluded infrastructure such as remote storage and data-center chillers [@tschand2025].

title: Data-Center Energy Efficiency Gains
caption: **Data-Center Energy Efficiency Gains**: Each series is normalized to its own first plotted version, so compare improvement within a workload rather than absolute efficiency across workloads. Source: [@tschand2025].
alt: Line chart of normalized energy efficiency across MLPerf Inference versions from 2021 to 2024. RetinaNet and ResNet rise to 3 times their initial values; BERT and GPT-J reach about 1.9 times, DLRM-v2 about 1.7 times, Llama 2 about 1.5 times, and RNN-T about 1.3 times.
context:
Standardizing the boundary prevents misleading comparisons across architectural families. By specifying instrumentation, measurement boundaries, matched logging windows, and the applicable workload constraints, MLPerf Power makes efficiency results interpretable within the tested scenario.

Over successive benchmark submission rounds from 2021 to 2024, standardized measurements capture how architectural improvements, compiler optimizations, and lower-precision arithmetic translate into production efficiency gains. Tracking normalized energy efficiency (samples per joule) across eight submission cycles from v1.0 to v4.1, @fig-power-trends charts diverging efficiency trajectories across seven distinct MLPerf Inference workloads.

title: Hardware-Dependent Latency–Accuracy Trade-offs
caption: **Hardware-Dependent Latency–Accuracy Trade-offs**: Each panel holds top-1 ImageNet accuracy on the vertical axis while using a target-specific latency scale horizontally. The arrow links MobileNetV3 Large at roughly equal accuracy on CPU float and DSP, exposing the hardware-dependent latency shift. Source: [@chu2021].
alt: Five scatter plots compare top-1 ImageNet accuracy with latency on Pixel 4 CPU float, CPU uint8, GPU, EdgeTPU, and DSP targets for eight model families. An arrow links approximately equal-accuracy points on the CPU-float and DSP panels.
context:
[^fn-hardware-lottery-hooker]: **Hardware lottery**\index{Hardware lottery!benchmark bias}: Coined by @hooker2021 to describe how algorithmic success depends on alignment with available hardware and software. Transformer workloads benefit from dense matrix operations that map efficiently to modern accelerators, while graph neural networks and sparse mixture-of-experts models can be harder to evaluate when available silicon and software stacks favor dense kernels. Hardware-specific leaderboards therefore favor architectures aligned with the measured platform and may obscure alternatives that would fare differently under other hardware assumptions.

Hardware compatibility dependence introduces systematic biases when evaluating models across heterogeneous execution targets. An architecture optimized for GPU execution may underperform on an embedded CPU, DSP, or custom edge accelerator with differing vector widths, cache hierarchies, and quantization support. Across five hardware targets on a Google Pixel 4, @fig-hw-lottery charts how the latency–accuracy Pareto frontier reshuffles between CPU float, CPU uint8, GPU, EdgeTPU, and DSP execution. The diagonal purple arrow links MobileNetV3 Large at roughly 75 percent top-1 accuracy, from approximately 20 ms on CPU float to 4.5 ms on the DSP. Multi-MAX reaches roughly 75 percent accuracy at 2.2 ms on EdgeTPU and 3.4 ms on DSP; its points at higher accuracy carry higher latency. Comparisons must therefore match both the model variant and the accuracy operating point. The shifted frontiers show why model selection requires measurements on the target execution path rather than a latency ranking inherited from another processor.

title: Performance Spectrum
caption: **Performance Spectrum**: Scientific and edge applications occupy widely separated operating points in data rate and available computation time, motivating benchmarks tied to each application's timing and data-movement constraints. Source: [@duarte2022fastml].
alt: Log-scale scatter plot of data rate vs. computation time for LHC sensors and triggers, scientific instruments and controls, Internet of Things systems, and mobile devices. Points and error bars span roughly 10^4 to 10^14 bytes per second and nanoseconds to fractions of a second, with a shaded Fast ML for Science benchmark region.
context:
Early deep learning benchmarks evaluated image classification and object detection on convolutional networks. As workloads expanded to large language models, recommendation systems, and generative AI\index{Generative AI!benchmark evolution}, those vision benchmarks failed to capture long-context attention, autoregressive decoding, and sparse expert routing, and community benchmarks moved to language understanding [@wang2018; @wang2019superglue] and foundation model capabilities [@liang2022helm]. How saturation erodes a static benchmark's discriminating power is a data question, taken up in @sec-benchmarking-data-benchmarking-22f9.

Benchmark evolution also expands the dimensions of measurement. While early benchmarks focused on throughput and accuracy, contemporary systems require multi-objective evaluation across energy efficiency, memory footprint, and tail latency under resource constraints. Scientific instruments provide a further constraint regime in @fig-sciml-graph. Its shaded "Fast ML for Science" envelope places high-throughput trigger pipelines outside typical mobile and IoT operating points [@duarte2022fastml]. The distance between these operating points is why a benchmark must match its application.

title: Development Paradigms
caption: **Development Paradigms**: Model-centric AI iterates on architecture while holding the dataset fixed, whereas data-centric AI iterates on annotations, diversity, and bias while holding the architecture fixed. The double arrow marks the approaches as complementary.
alt: Side-by-side diagrams: model-centric AI shows data cylinders feeding CPU with feedback loop to model, data-centric AI shows feedback loop to data instead. Double arrow indicates complementary approaches.
context:
:::

Distribution alignment challenges highlight a persistent tension in ML development between two paradigms: *fixing the data and iterating on models*, or *fixing the model and iterating on data*. The side-by-side schematics in @fig-model-vs-data isolate this divergence through the placement of the padlock and feedback path. In the model-centric panel\index{Model-centric AI!architectural innovation}, the dataset is locked while the feedback loop iteratively refines model parameters on the CPU; in the data-centric panel, the model architecture is locked while the loop routes back to enhance training data quality, diversity, and labeling. As the bidirectional red arrow emphasizes, the two paradigms are complementary engineering strategies rather than mutually exclusive philosophies.

title: Dataset Saturation
caption: **Dataset Saturation**: The zero line denotes reported human performance; each curve's crossing marks a capability for which the static benchmark has less remaining discriminating headroom. The crossings do not distinguish genuine capability gains from optimization to the evaluation set. Sources: [@perrault2024artificial; @kiela2021].
alt: Line chart showing five AI capabilities crossing human performance baseline from 1998 to 2020: handwriting, speech, image recognition, reading comprehension, and language understanding.
context:
#### Dataset saturation and dynamic benchmarks {.unnumbered}

Even when coverage, quality, and distribution alignment protocols are satisfied, static benchmarks encounter the problem of dataset saturation\index{Dataset saturation!performance capability illusion}. As models approach empirical upper bounds on fixed test suites, leaderboard deltas compress, making it difficult to distinguish genuine capability advances from over-optimization to benchmark-specific artifacts. The capability trajectories in @fig-dataset-saturation plot this exhaustion over two decades, showing AI scores rising from normalized baselines (-100) to cross the zero line marking human performance [@perrault2024artificial]. While handwriting and speech recognition required over a decade to reach human parity (the green shaded region), reading comprehension and language understanding surged across the threshold in under two years between 2016 and 2020, rapidly exhausting the discriminating headroom of static suites.

title: The Inference Pipeline
caption: **The Inference Pipeline**: ML serving systems transform raw inputs into final outputs through sequential stages: preprocessing, neural network computation, and postprocessing. The neural network represents just one component; preprocessing and postprocessing make end-to-end latency depend on more than neural-network execution.
alt: Left-to-right flow diagram of six connected boxes labeled Raw Data, Pre-processing, Neural Network, Raw Output, Post-processing, and Final Output. Outlined groups beneath the boxes identify Pre-processing, Deep Learning, and Post-processing.
context:
:::

[^fn-slo-sla-serving]: **SLOs in ML serving**\index{SLO!vs. SLA}\index{SLO!multidimensional targets}: An SLO is the internal target, as distinct from the contractual SLA. For ML serving, task quality and inference latency can both contribute to SLOs, creating multidimensional targets where improving one dimension (for example, deploying a larger model for accuracy) can violate another (latency).

title: Inference Server Anatomy
caption: **Inference Server Anatomy**: A modern inference server decouples network handling from accelerator execution through a staged pipeline. Each stage isolates a concern, from absorbing bursty traffic to forming efficient batches, so the hardware accelerator stays highly utilized despite irregular arrival patterns.
alt: Flowchart showing a six-stage inference server pipeline: client to network ingress to request queue to dynamic batcher, then down to inference runner to accelerator. Arrows connect stages sequentially.
context:
An inference server\index{Inference server!architecture}[^fn-inference-server-serving] (such as NVIDIA Triton or TensorFlow Serving) functions as a specialized runtime scheduler that manages concurrency, device memory, and data movement between host CPUs and accelerator devices. Rather than invoking model execution synchronously upon request arrival, the server pipelines incoming requests through dedicated subsystems that isolate client network handling from accelerator compute. Every request traverses a multi-stage runtime pipeline designed to maximize hardware throughput while bounding queuing latency. In six stages (@fig-server-anatomy), incoming client queries traverse network ingress and request-buffering queues before the dynamic batcher stages them downward to the inference runner and the hardware accelerator.

[^fn-inference-server-serving]: **Inference server**\index{Inference server!serving architecture}: Google's TensorFlow Serving\index{TensorFlow Serving!inference server} [@olston2017tensorflow] helped establish the separation of model logic from serving infrastructure; NVIDIA's Triton\index{Triton!inference server} [@nvidia_triton] extends this pattern across multiple model frameworks and backends. The critical design insight is that a scheduler and dynamic batcher turn irregular single-request traffic into accelerator-friendly execution, improving utilization when latency budgets allow batching. Exact utilization gains depend on model, hardware, arrival rate, and the configured batching window.
