Laid on the node's hardware, the same budget occupies three resources in turn, and the accelerator is busy for less than half of the request (@fig-model-serving-request-timeline).

title: Request Pipelining
caption: **Request Pipelining**: Pipelining hides latency by overlapping independent operations across different hardware resources. In pipelined execution (B), the CPU processes the next request's data while the GPU executes the current request's inference. This can increase accelerator duty cycle and throughput without changing the model.
alt: Two timing diagrams. A (Serial): alternating CPU preprocessing, GPU inference, and idle blocks in sequence. B (Pipelined): two parallel rows where CPU preprocessing overlaps with GPU inference, eliminating idle time.
context:
#### Overlapping I/O and compute {#sec-model-serving-overlapping-io-compute-966c}

@Fig-serving-pipeline-timing sequences execution across CPU preprocessing and GPU inference to demonstrate how request pipelining recovers lost compute capacity. In serial execution (A), each request must complete its entire lifecycle (Network $\rightarrow$ CPU Preprocessing $\rightarrow$ GPU Inference $\rightarrow$ Postprocessing) before the next request begins, leaving the GPU idle for more than 50 percent of wall-clock time. Pipelining concurrent requests (B) overlaps CPU preprocessing of upcoming requests with active GPU inference on earlier inputs, eliminating the idle bubbles and maximizing accelerator duty cycle.

Mean latency (blue) and the p99 approximation (red) both grow nonlinearly as utilization approaches saturation; the 70 percent marker is an illustrative planning knee rather than a model-derived breakpoint. In an $\KendallMarkovianCode/\KendallMarkovianCode/1$ queue, the 99th percentile latency scales as $-\ln(0.01) \approx 4.6\times$ mean latency, illustrating why tail delays compound violently near saturation.

title: The Throughput-Latency Knee
caption: **The Throughput-Latency Knee**: Batch size vs. throughput (blue) and latency (orange) for the reference ResNet-50 profile on the H100. Throughput rises nearly in proportion to batch size while fixed overhead dominates, then flattens toward its ceiling. Latency grows slowly at first and roughly in proportion to batch size beyond the marked planning knee, where it is twice the batch-one latency and throughput reaches half its ceiling. Each throughput value is batch size divided by the plotted formation-plus-service latency, for a single worker that waits out a 10 ms window and then serves each batch; pipelined serving sustains higher throughput. Values are modeled, not measured.
alt: Dual-axis line chart on a log batch-size axis. Blue line (throughput) rises steeply and then flattens. Orange line (latency) stays nearly flat through batch 32 and then climbs. A vertical dashed line labeled Planning Knee marks batch size near 400.
context: batching window requires a mean formation-plus-inference budget of approximately `{python} BatchThroughputCalc.batch8_budget_ms_str`: an arriving request waits on average half the window (`{python} BatchThroughputCalc.half_window_ms_str`, as derived in @sec-model-serving-queue-waiting-time-analysis-8d5c) and requires `{python} BatchThroughputCalc.batch8_inference_ms_str` of inference. If the service must meet a `{python} BatchThroughputCalc.slo_ms_str` SLO, the remaining `{python} BatchThroughputCalc.batch8_headroom_ms_str` provides headroom for worker backlog and auxiliary pipeline stages, while delivering `{python} BatchThroughputCalc.batch8_vs_batch1_mult_str` higher service throughput than batch 1 on identical hardware. On this accelerator the batching window, not the computation, is most of the batch-8 budget. Batch size cannot grow indefinitely, and @fig-throughput-latency-knee shows why by modeling this relationship across batch sizes on a logarithmic axis. To isolate the planning knee under worst-case scheduling conditions, the figure assumes a strictly serialized single worker that waits out the full batching window before executing each batch, without pipelined overlap ($\text{Latency} = \BatchingWindow + \BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)$). Under this unpipelined assumption, batch-1 throughput is `{python} BatchThroughputCalc.serial_b1_rps_str` rather than the `{python} BatchThroughputCalc.b1_rps_str` sustained when inference runs back to back. Throughput rises almost in proportion to batch size while the fixed overhead dominates each batch, because each added image costs only `{python} ResNetH100Profile.per_image_fp16_us_str` of device time. The planning knee sits where the batch's total per-image work equals the fixed part of its latency, the window plus the fixed cost, near batch `{python} BatchThroughputCalc.knee_batch_str`: there latency is twice that of batch one and throughput is half its ceiling, and beyond it each doubling of the batch roughly doubles latency while throughput gains less and less. In this model throughput never declines; it saturates, so latency, not throughput, sets the largest useful batch.

title: Framework Interoperability
caption: **Framework Interoperability**: The inward spokes represent exports into the shared ONNX format, while the outward spokes represent loads into compatible tools and runtimes; portability requires support on both sides of that boundary.
alt: Hub diagram with ONNX at center. Left side (export): PyTorch, TensorFlow, Keras, Caffe2, MXNet, Microsoft CNTK with arrows pointing inward. Right side (load): ONNX Runtime plus the same six frameworks with arrows pointing outward.
context:
The development framework and deployment runtime need not be the same system, but they must exchange a representation both can interpret. The **ONNX**\index{ONNX!definition}\index{ONNX!cross-framework portability} format addresses this fragmentation by standardizing model exchange across runtimes [@bai2019onnx]. A pipeline can train an architecture in PyTorch, export the computation graph to an ONNX intermediate representation, and execute the serialized graph in ONNX Runtime or compile it for a target accelerator. In contrast, TensorFlow Lite relies on its own conversion path, translating TensorFlow SavedModels into FlatBuffers rather than routing through ONNX. Although standard interchange formats reduce manual model conversion between development and production environments, they do not eliminate compatibility testing, operator coverage gaps, or custom-kernel fallback overhead.

The exchange is hub-and-spoke\index{ONNX!hub-and-spoke interoperability} around the common ONNX intermediate representation (@fig-onnx). Training frameworks such as PyTorch, TensorFlow, Keras, Caffe2, MXNet, and CNTK export inward to the shared representation, and ONNX Runtime and other target frameworks load the serialized computation graph outward without reimplementing model code.

title: The KV-Cache Explosion
caption: **The KV-Cache Explosion**: FP16 KV-cache usage vs. context length for a 70-billion-parameter-class model with GQA. On the modeled H100's 80 GB of HBM (85.9 GB decimal), 35.3 GB of INT4 weights leave 50.6 GB for KV cache before runtime overhead. Batch size 32 reaches that cache budget at roughly 4.8k tokens, forcing a trade-off between batch size and context length.
alt: Line chart of FP16 KV-cache size against context length for batch sizes 1, 4, 16, and 32. All four lines rise linearly, with steeper slopes for larger batches. A red dashed horizontal line marks the cache budget remaining after the INT4 weights on the modeled H100; batch size 32 crosses it near 4.8k tokens. The region above the budget line is shaded red and labeled Out of Memory (OOM) Zone.
context:
Once contexts grow, the cache rather than the weights sets how many conversations one accelerator can hold, and Llama 3 8B makes the budget concrete. Each token stores a key vector and a value vector in every layer for every key-value head. Storing 16-bit Key and Value tensors across $\LayerCount=32$ layers with $\KvHeadCount=8$ grouped-query attention heads of dimension $\AttentionHeadDimension=128$ requires $2 \times 32 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2\text{ bytes} = 131{,}072\text{ bytes} \approx 131\text{ KB}$ per token per sequence. Grouped-query attention [@dubey2024llama] lets the model's `{python} KvBudget.heads_str` query heads share those key-value heads, which cuts the cache by `{python} KvBudget.mha_ratio_mult_str` relative to full multi-head attention. An `{python} KvBudget.context_tokens_str`-token conversation therefore holds `{python} KvBudget.kv_per_seq_gb_str`. With `{python} KvBudget.weights8_gb_str` of FP16 weights resident on an H100 whose `{python} KvBudget.capacity_gib_str` datasheet capacity is `{python} KvBudget.capacity_gb_str` in the decimal units used for tensor footprints, about `{python} KvBudget.free8_gb_str` remains for caches before runtime workspace, room for about `{python} KvBudget.n_seq_str` such conversations at once. The weights are a fixed cost; every additional conversation, and every additional thousand tokens of context, draws on the same remainder.

Larger models make the cache the binding constraint sooner. For a 70-billion-parameter-class model with grouped-query attention, 4-bit weights consume `{python} KvBudget.weights70_gb_str` of the same H100, leaving `{python} KvBudget.free70_gb_str` for FP16 cache before runtime workspace. A batch of `{python} KvBudget.batch_large_str` conversations exhausts that budget at roughly `{python} KvBudget.crossing70_str` tokens of context, so serving engines trade concurrent batch size against context length to avoid out-of-memory failures (@fig-kv-cache-growth).

The series is intended as a market trend indicator, not a controlled or current-price comparison. API token-processing prices have collapsed by multiple orders of magnitude, transforming the economics of automated AI workflows.

Blue points are labeled by model, and a red dashed trend line fitted through the cheapest price at each date slopes downward across the plot.
context:
:::

The same serving-economics pressure appears in public API prices. @Fig-intelligence-deflation tracks this cost collapse across representative public API list-price snapshots from 2023 through 2025 on a logarithmic scale. The steep downward trend line isolates how prompt token pricing fell by multiple orders of magnitude, from thirty dollars per million tokens for original GPT-4 down to several cents for Gemini 1.5 Flash and DeepSeek-V3. Vendor prices change frequently, so these points should be read as historical provenance for the trend rather than as current purchasing guidance [@openai2023chatgptwhisper; @openai2023gpt4web; @openaiCommunity2024gpt4oApi; @openai2024gpt4oMini; @anthropic2024claude3family; @google2024gemini15flashPricing; @deepseek2024v3]. Each order-of-magnitude drop changes which applications are economically viable, and a provider can sustain such prices only if its serving stack extracts more completed requests from each accelerator-hour. Converting engineering efficiency into unit cost draws on the latency, batching, and memory mechanisms of the preceding sections.

The degradation is measurable. In the Wild-Time benchmark, @yao2022wildtime train a model on data from one period and test it both on held-out data from that period and on data from later years, across six real datasets that span yearbook portraits, satellite imagery, hospital records, news, and scientific papers. @Fig-temporal-shift shows the result. The loss comes entirely from the world moving away from the training data, and only monitoring that compares predictions against fresh outcomes can see it.

title: Iterative MLOps Loop
caption: **Iterative MLOps Loop**: Monitoring and triggering feed production evidence back into design and model development, turning requirements, engineering, testing, and deployment into a continuous operating cycle.
alt: Infinity-loop diagram with three phases. Design phase: requirements, use-case prioritization, data availability. Model development: data engineering, model engineering, testing. Operations: deployment, CI/CD pipeline, monitoring and triggering.
context:
:::

The loop has three stages (design, model development, and operations), but its defining feature is the return path. Runtime telemetry and retraining triggers carry live performance signals from operations back into requirements and data engineering, so deployment feeds the next design cycle instead of ending the project (@fig-mlops-diagram).

title: Hidden Infrastructure of ML Systems
caption: **Hidden Infrastructure of ML Systems**: ML code is one of ten components arranged around the ML system at the center, alongside data collection, data verification, feature extraction, configuration, machine resource management, serving infrastructure, monitoring, analysis tools, and process management tools. Modeling occupies one circle and the remaining nine identify the operational surface a deployment must also carry; circle counts do not measure code volume or maintenance cost. Source: [@sculley2015hidden].
alt: Hub-and-spoke diagram with the ML system at the center, connected by arrows to ten surrounding components: data collection, data verification, feature extraction, configuration, machine resource management, serving infrastructure, monitoring, analysis tools, process management tools, and ML code.
context:
:::

The debt is larger than manual retraining alone, because modeling code constitutes only a small fraction of a real-world deployment. Core modeling code is one peripheral component among ten around the ML system, alongside nine supporting subsystems spanning data verification, feature extraction, configuration, and machine resource management (@fig-technical-debt). Their presence broadens the maintenance surface; the diagram does not measure each component's cost.

title: Correction Cascades
caption: **Correction Cascades**: Each model is trained to correct the errors of the model before it, forming a chain of dependencies. Changing an upstream model can invalidate downstream corrections, turning one local fix into revalidation across the chain and potentially several retraining cycles.
alt: Four model boxes in a left-to-right chain labeled Model A through Model D, each trained to correct the previous one. A red change badge on Model A and red dashed arcs reaching Model B, C, and D show an upstream change propagating downstream, with must revalidate labels beneath the downstream models.
context:
When boundary erosion goes unaddressed, engineering interventions frequently trigger a **correction cascade**\index{Correction cascade!sequential dependencies}: fixing a specific model defect with an auxiliary patch introduces secondary errors elsewhere, requiring further compensatory fixes that destabilize the entire pipeline. In ML systems, these cascades are severe because changes propagate through statistical dependencies rather than deterministic code branches. Retraining a model to correct a specific false-positive cluster may degrade accuracy across previously stable cohorts. Adding an auxiliary model to override edge-case predictions introduces uncalibrated residuals that distort downstream consumers. Repeated dependent patches can demand coordinated revalidation, with maintenance costs that may exceed those of revising the base model.

@Fig-correction-cascades-flowchart traces this failure propagation along a four-stage dependency chain (Models A through D), where each downstream component compensates for the residual errors of its predecessor. When an upstream patch alters Model A, the dashed red arcs mark every downstream correction that requires revalidation and may need retraining.

title: MLOps Stack Layers
caption: **MLOps Stack Layers**: Five columns organize the ML system stack: ML Models/Applications, ML Frameworks/Platforms, Model Orchestration, Infrastructure, and Hardware. MLOps spans orchestration tasks from data management through model serving and infrastructure tasks from job scheduling through monitoring, supporting automation, reproducibility, and scalable deployment.
alt: Layered architecture diagram. Top row: ML models, frameworks, orchestration, infrastructure, hardware. MLOps section spans orchestration tasks (data management through model serving) and infrastructure tasks (job scheduling through monitoring).
context:
These operational components sit between the framework and the hardware and track what neither of them tracks, the data lineage and the cluster state. MLOps occupies the middle of the five-tier stack of @fig-ops-layers (ML models, frameworks, orchestration, infrastructure, and hardware). Model orchestration, which runs from data management to serving, and operational infrastructure, which runs from job scheduling to monitoring, together bridge mathematical frameworks and physical accelerator clusters and enforce the remediations of @tbl-mlops-infrastructure-debt. The tiers say *where* a component sits in the implementation stack, while the four layers of @tbl-mlops-layers say *who* owns an operational responsibility; the rest of the chapter reasons with the layers and the three interfaces.

Inside the orchestration and infrastructure tiers, four architectural mechanisms execute these operational responsibilities. First, a feature storage and retrieval layer serves a unified schema across two disparate access patterns: high-throughput analytical scans over immutable columnar files for offline training, and low-latency point lookups against key-value stores for online serving (@sec-ml-operations-feature-stores-c01c). Second, an artifact and lineage store records content-addressed hashes for dataset snapshots, code commits, container images, and model weights, ensuring any live prediction can be audited back to its exact training inputs (@sec-ml-operations-versioning-lineage-b1cf). Third, workflow orchestration sequences pipeline stages, from ingestion and validation through training and evaluation, as declared dependency graphs with retry semantics and automated triggers (@sec-ml-operations-cicd-pipelines-a9de). Fourth, a compute runtime schedules accelerator hardware, host memory, and processor cores across training jobs and serving endpoints under strict resource isolation (@sec-ml-operations-training-pipelines-2dcf). Specific frameworks implement pieces of this decomposition, but the underlying mechanisms and interface boundaries outlast any particular tool.

title: ML CI/CD Pipeline
caption: **ML CI/CD Pipeline**: Read the enclosed stages in execution order; the retraining trigger starts a new run, while connected repositories preserve the dataset, model, metadata, and artifacts needed to reproduce and govern it. Adapted from Google Cloud's MLOps continuous delivery and automation pipeline guidance [@googleCloudMlopsPipelines].
alt: Pipeline diagram labeled Continuous training pipeline. Seven stages connect dataset ingestion, data validation, data transformation, model training/tuning, model evaluation, model validation, and model registration. A dataset and feature repository connects on the left, a model repository on the right, an ML metadata and artifact repository above, and a retraining trigger above the pipeline. Three boxes below are labeled model processing engine, model training engine, and model evaluation engine.
context:
Without this automation, model deployment degrades into a manual, error-prone process in which an engineer retrains locally, copies artifacts to a staging server, and promotes to production with no guarantee that the data, code, or hyperparameters match what was validated. The cost of such ad hoc workflows compounds with team size and deployment frequency, producing configuration drift and silent regressions that surface only after the model has served incorrect predictions.

A continuous training pipeline runs seven sequential stages, from dataset ingestion, data validation, and data transformation through training, evaluation, validation, and registry promotion (@fig-ops-cicd). Driven by dedicated processing, training, and evaluation engines beneath the pipeline, the workflow coordinates with surrounding dataset, model, and metadata repositories whenever an external trigger initiates retraining.

title: Data Drift Impact
caption: **Data Drift Impact**: In this illustrative scenario, incoming samples shift from predominantly online to increasingly offline sales while model accuracy declines over the same interval. Monitoring inputs and outcomes together helps determine whether the distribution shift is associated with the loss in accuracy.
alt: Three horizontally aligned panels over time. The top panel shows incoming samples as green and orange blocks. The middle panel shows the sales_channel feature distribution changing from a green Online store region to an expanding orange Offline store region. The bottom panel shows a green model-accuracy curve declining from left to right.
context:
Operations adds one distinction that the definitions alone do not make. **Model decay**\index{Model decay!definition} is the observed decline in prediction quality over time while the model code stays unchanged, and data drift is only one possible cause of it, alongside concept drift and changes in the surrounding pipeline. Monitoring model outputs alone can miss input drift or mistake a benign output change for quality loss, so operations also tracks the input feature statistics behind the divergence $\StatisticalDivergence$, using the distance measures of feature distribution monitoring (@sec-ml-operations-feature-distribution-monitoring-b8a0). These statistics can warn earlier than labeled performance because ground-truth feedback is often delayed.

The signature of data drift in live telemetry is a feature distribution that moves in step with a quality metric, and three synchronized telemetry tiers aligned over time expose how covariate shift erodes model performance (@fig-data-drift). Across the top panel, discrete request samples transition from predominantly green (online sales) to orange (in-store sales); the figure's "online store" and "offline store" labels name sales channels, not the feature-store tiers of @sec-ml-operations-feature-stores-c01c. The middle panel charts this shift as an expanding offline area in the sales_channel feature distribution, directly matching the steep decline of the model accuracy curve in the bottom panel. This temporal alignment motivates comparing input feature distributions with outcome metrics; their co-movement supplies a diagnostic hypothesis rather than establishing the cause by itself.

After the run, the candidate it produces can go out as a canary on `{python} ReleaseControlFootprint.accels_per_copy_str` of the freed accelerators. The schedule is illustrative and built from the chapter's worked numbers.

The bottom four lanes hold a retraining run for the first six hours. After the run, two of those lanes hold a canary copy and the last two are drawn as a dashed outline marked free.
context:
```

The run cost $\RetrainingRunCost$ bundles the four terms of @eq-retrain-cost, and on the ranking service the accelerator term is the smallest of them. In an illustrative scenario, a run that retrains on the logs gathered since the previous run occupies four H100s for six hours. Those twenty-four accelerator-hours cost `{python} RetrainContention.compute_cost_str` at the registry's training rate, about `{python} RetrainContention.compute_share_pct_str` of the `{python} RetrainContention.run_cost_str` run. Validation, deployment, and rollout risk make up the rest, which is why automating the validation path (@sec-ml-operations-model-validation-a891) shortens the economic interval more than faster training would. The accelerator-hours matter instead as contention. The serving copy of the tables already holds two accelerators, so on an eight-accelerator node a run that holds its own copy and training state on four more leaves room for exactly one further copy of the tables while it executes (@fig-ml-ops-dlrm-node-day). That copy can be a canary, a shadow, or the hot standby of @tbl-ml-ops-release-control-footprint, but not more than one of them, so a team that releases and retrains on the same node must schedule the two so that a retraining run never evicts the copy that makes rollback immediate.

title: The Rotting Asset Curve
caption: **The Rotting Asset Curve**: An illustrative exponential accuracy decay under two maintenance policies, both drawn as sawtooths. The scheduled policy resets every 90 days regardless of accuracy and dips below the drift threshold before each reset, while the triggered policy resets on crossing that threshold and holds a higher floor in this zero-delay model. Real response delays and update quality must be measured; neither cadence is universal.
alt: Line chart of model accuracy vs. days since deployment. An orange scheduled-retraining sawtooth resets every 90 days, a green trigger-based sawtooth resets when it crosses a red dashed drift-threshold line, and both begin at 0.94 accuracy, the ranking service at launch.
context:
### Scheduled versus triggered retraining {#sec-ml-operations-scheduled-triggered-retraining-b51e}

The interval above fixes a schedule, while the triggered policy of @sec-ml-operations-retraining-decision-framework-e33d lets evidence decide when to run. Over a 365-day deployment the two policies trace different sawtooths against a drift threshold of 0.88 accuracy (@fig-rotting-asset-curve)\index{Rotting asset curve!accuracy decay}. Under a scheduled policy (orange sawtooth), the model retrains at rigid 90-day intervals, repeatedly dipping below the quality floor before each reset. In contrast, a triggered policy (green sawtooth) initiates retraining the moment monitored accuracy touches the threshold, illustrating an idealized instantaneous reset; in practice the trigger is often a divergence or proxy signal calibrated against accuracy. Both curves are drawn from the temporal decay model of @eq-accuracy-decay. In deployment, sample collection, label arrival, training, validation, and rollout delays can carry accuracy below the trigger before recovery; the policy does not guarantee a performance floor.

title: The Business Cost Curve
caption: **The Business Cost Curve**: An equal-class-weighted illustrative cost index vs. classification threshold. Technical metrics like ROC curves hide the economic reality: errors have different costs. Here, a false negative (missed fraud) costs \$500, while a false positive (blocked user) costs \$100. The system flags a transaction as fraud when its score exceeds the threshold, so a lower threshold flags more transactions. Because missing fraud is $5\times$ more costly, the optimal threshold shifts left of center, making the system more aggressive at flagging suspicious transactions and accepting more false positives to minimize expensive misses. With equal costs the optimum would sit at threshold = 0.50; the asymmetry pulls it toward threshold $\approx 0.34$. A population expected cost would also weight each term by class prevalence. MLOps tunes thresholds as costs and prevalence change.
alt: Line chart showing an equal-class-weighted illustrative cost index vs. classification threshold from 0 to 1. Three curves are plotted: false positive cost index (dashed blue) decreasing sigmoidally from left to right, false negative cost index (dashed red) increasing sigmoidally from left to right, and total cost index (solid violet) as their sum forming a U-shape. The optimal threshold is marked with a green dot left of center where the total index is minimized.
context:
A frequent communication failure is the unconstrained request to "make the model more accurate." Model accuracy cannot be scaled independently of system costs. Boosting validation accuracy by two percentage points often requires moving to a significantly larger model architecture, incurring higher FLOP counts per sample, increasing memory bandwidth demands, and violating strict inference latency SLOs. Grounding improvement discussions in the Pareto frontier (principle \ref{pri-pareto-frontier}) forces explicit decisions among model accuracy, inference latency budgets, training compute costs, and dataset acquisition expenses.

Translating statistical metrics into operational impact requires mapping errors to their consequences, which are rarely symmetric. Accuracy, ROC-AUC, and F1 treat errors symmetrically. The ranking service's errors differ in cost only mildly, so a separate illustrative case with a sharper asymmetry carries the argument. In an automated fraud detection pipeline, a false positive creates friction at checkout while a false negative allows unrecoverable theft. With missed fraud (\$500 per incident) five times as costly as a blocked legitimate user (\$100), the total cost across classification thresholds reaches its minimum near 0.34, well left of the symmetric 0.50 baseline (@fig-business-cost-curve).

title: Uptime Dependency Stack
caption: **Uptime Dependency Stack**: The waterline separates visible service uptime from data- and model-health failures that can remain hidden while the service stays available; the surrounding labels organize the monitoring surface into data, model, and service health.
alt: Iceberg diagram with uptime visible above waterline. Hidden below: model accuracy, data drift, concept drift, broken pipelines, schema changes, model bias, data outages, underperforming segments. Labels indicate data, model, and service health.
context:
The repeatable ranking service above already automates training and deployment, yet a change to its separately maintained feature SQL still requires manual validation. More frequent retraining would increase the manual validation burden without removing the mismatch risk. A versioned feature contract and matched-request parity tests address the failure boundary first; a shared feature store becomes useful when maintaining that contract across pipelines warrants the additional infrastructure. Maturity assessment therefore selects the next missing control for each system.

@Fig-uptime-iceberg provides a coverage map for that assessment. Service uptime is visible at the tip, while data- and model-health failures can remain hidden below the waterline. For each failure mode, the assessment must identify the evidence that exposes it and the action that contains it.

context:
#### Feedback loops {#sec-ml-operations-feedback-loops-3cdd}

Three interlocking feedback loops organize the proposed integration of machine learning into clinical practice; their effectiveness and safety require validation in the intended setting. @Fig-clinaiops models these three interlocking feedback loops as a triangular protocol among the patient, clinician, and AI developer. Each pair of actors exchanges different information in both directions: the patient streams wearable sensor telemetry and receives clinician-approved therapy alerts; the AI developer provides longitudinal monitoring summaries while accepting physician-defined dosing bounds; and the clinician directly governs patient therapy regimens while establishing safety boundaries for algorithmic actuation. The outer cycle connecting all three nodes forms the overarching clinical governance framework.

Each panel shows paired arrows between two icons and text boxes describing blood-pressure monitoring, dose recommendations, clinician limits, risk alerts, trend review, adverse-event checks, and lifestyle factors.

##### Loop implementation {#sec-ml-operations-loop-implementation-2556}

The hypertension workflow labels each of its three panels by the two parties in the exchange (@fig-interactive-loop), so the panels do not line up one-to-one with the three loops of @fig-clinaiops. title: The Responsible Engineering Lifecycle
caption: **The Responsible Engineering Lifecycle**: Four chained stages carry the credit service from requirement to production. Specify fixes the target, the named populations, and the oversight boundary; Measure turns them into release gates; Explain and document makes decisions and models legible; Operate watches the deployed model and feeds what it observes back into the next specification. Resource and Govern span every stage: each stage consumes accelerator-hours, energy, and money, and each must leave evidence that someone outside the team can audit. The machine cost under each stage names what the remedy consumes.
alt: Four boxes left to right labeled Specify, Measure, Explain and document, and Operate, joined by arrows, with a return arrow from Operate back to Specify labeled feedback and retraining. Under each box a short gray line names its machine cost: labeled evaluation data per named group and reviewer hours, per-slice evaluation and mitigation training, explanation compute on the serving path, and per-group telemetry and exploration traffic. Two long bars beneath all four boxes are labeled Resource: energy, carbon, and cost of every stage, and Govern: access control, privacy, lineage, and audit evidence for every stage.
context:
care-management algorithm were both found to fail after the design options that could have addressed them were closed, so the lesson concerns timing more than vigilance. Each responsibility failure in this chapter has a point in the ML lifecycle before which it is cheap to prevent and after which it becomes expensive or impossible to repair, so responsible engineering\index{Responsible engineering!lifecycle methodology} is organized around that lifecycle rather than around a list of concerns.

Six stages follow from that premise, and the first four form a chain in which each stage depends on the output of the one before it. *Specify* comes first because a system cannot be tested against a requirement nobody wrote down; the target, the populations that matter, the evaluation data those populations demand, and the boundary of human oversight must all be fixed before training forecloses the alternatives. *Measure* turns those written requirements into release gates, evaluating each named population separately and quantifying the trade-offs among fairness criteria. Evidence that lives only in an engineer's notebook cannot be contested, audited, or reused, so *Explain and document* makes individual decisions legible to the people they affect and whole models legible to the teams that inherit them. The documented operating envelope then tells *Operate* what to watch after launch, when feedback loops and distribution shift erode a model that passed every gate. The last two stages span the whole lifecycle rather than following it, so each receives its own section, while the four chained stages structure the subsections of this one, each worked on the credit service. *Resource* accounts for the energy, carbon, and money that every stage consumes (@sec-responsible-engineering-environmental-cost-awareness-0f3e), and *Govern* supplies the regulatory obligations and the data infrastructure of access control, privacy, lineage, and audit that make each earlier stage provable to someone outside the team that built it (@sec-responsible-engineering-data-governance-compliance-bd1a). The four chained stages and the two that span them form one loop (@fig-responsible-lifecycle).

title: Threshold Effects on Subgroup Outcomes
caption: **Threshold Effects on Subgroup Outcomes**: Two candidate classification thresholds intersect different score distributions for Subgroups A and B. Circles mark positive outcomes (loan repayment), plus markers mark negative outcomes (default), and color distinguishes subgroup; each boundary approves the markers to its left. Each dashed line carries the overall accuracy that boundary achieves, not a score cutoff. Moving to the higher-accuracy boundary lifts overall accuracy from 75 percent to 81.25 percent, but the whole gain falls in Subgroup A, which becomes perfectly separated, while Subgroup B goes from one misclassification to three.
alt: Two horizontal rows labeled Subgroup A and Subgroup B contain colored circle and plus markers at different positions. Dashed vertical lines labeled 75 percent and 81.25 percent cross both rows. Circles denote positive outcomes, plus signs denote negative outcomes, and color identifies subgroup.
section: Compare groups and flag disparities exceeding threshold
context:
: **Fairness Metrics Summary**: In the constructed credit-service scenario, approval rate and true positive rate differ across groups, while false positive rates match; the table establishes disparity but not its cause. {#tbl-fairness-metrics-summary tbl-colwidths="[40,20,20,20]"}

Shared classification thresholds applied to differing score distributions illustrate how aggregate performance masks severe subgroup divergence [@barocas2016]. Shifting between the two candidate decision boundaries (@fig-fairness-threshold) lifts overall accuracy from 75 percent to 81.25 percent by achieving perfect separation in Subgroup A, yet simultaneously triples the misclassifications in Subgroup B. Because the two subgroups' scores are distributed differently, one shared boundary cannot sit at the best point for both, and the move that raises the global metric does so by trading away Subgroup B's outcomes. Aggregate accuracy alone cannot determine whether those outcomes are equitable for either cohort.

#### Quantifying the fairness-accuracy trade-off {#sec-responsible-engineering-quantifying-fairnessaccuracy-tradeoff-ce4a}

The worked example showed that fairness criteria can conflict. A separate question is how a chosen engineering constraint changes predictive utility. The Pareto frontier (principle \ref{pri-pareto-frontier}) collects the configurations for which one plotted objective cannot improve without degrading another. @Fig-fairness-frontier plots a hypothetical fairness-accuracy Pareto frontier\index{Pareto frontier!fairness-accuracy trade-off}\index{Fairness!accuracy trade-off} against demographic disparity, measured as the difference between two groups' positive-prediction (approval) rates, the demographic parity gap defined in @sec-responsible-engineering-worked-example-fairness-analysis-loan-approval-2c72. Whatever the requirement, the candidate models lie along a gradient continuum from intrinsic interpretability to post-hoc explanation (@fig-interpretability-spectrum). title: Data Governance Framework
caption: **Data Governance Framework**: Eight operating elements surround Data Governance as a central hub: policies, organization, security, operations, data quality and master data, sourcing, catalogs, and shared analytic definitions. The circular arrangement presents governance as a coordinated operating model rather than a single control, spanning organizational functions such as catalogs, sourcing, and analytic definitions alongside technical controls such as data security. Adapted from standard enterprise data governance frameworks.
alt: Circular diagram with 'Data Governance' at center, surrounded by eight topical elements: Organization, Policies, Data catalogs, Data & analytic definitions, Data Sourcing, Data quality & master Data, Data Operations, Data Security.
context:
Compliance translates jurisdiction-specific statutes (such as GDPR, CCPA, and LGPD) into hard architectural constraints that govern pipeline retention windows, consent verification, and cross-border data replication. For KWS, compliance begins by determining the applicable legal basis and the scope of a revocation or erasure request. Authorized workflows then remove or restrict in-scope voice profiles and acoustic data according to documented retention and backup policies, with evidence of completion. Lineage and audit systems construct the trails that render the entire data lifecycle inspectable. Retained lineage linking deployed weights through training snapshots to authorized source records supports verification of security claims and applicable obligations, and its required detail depends on the use case and the evidence that must be reconstructed. In the KWS pipeline, lineage establishes provenance through content hashes and signed manifests that link each deployed DS-CNN binary back through specific training splits and acoustic augmentation seeds to the original raw recordings.

Governance works as an operating model rather than a single control. The framework in @fig-data-governance-pillars arranges eight elements, from organizational oversight and compliance policies to data catalogs, sourcing, quality metrics, runtime operations, and security, around a central governance hub. Technical mechanisms and organizational processes must function as mutually reinforcing subsystems: encrypted storage without identity-mapped access controls remains vulnerable to unauthorized exfiltration, and compliant storage without verifiable audit trails cannot survive regulatory inspection. Within the D·A·M taxonomy, data governance is the control plane of the Data axis. It enforces lawful provenance, privacy bounds, and lifecycle integrity for the data that feeds the Algorithm, and it runs on Machine-axis infrastructure such as encrypted storage, access control, and audit logs.

caption: **Responsible AI Governance Layers**: Four nested ovals place team-level safeguards at the center, surrounded by organizational safety culture, industry certification and review, and government regulation. The nesting distinguishes implementation at the center from oversight outside it; the annotation states that requirements flow inward and technical practices enable compliance. Adapted from @shneiderman2022human.
alt: Four nested ovals labeled, from center outward: Team—Reliable Systems, Organization—Safety culture and organization design, Industry—Trustworthy certification and external reviews, and Government Regulation—laws, executive orders, regulatory agencies. The team layer lists audit trails, verification and bias testing, explainable interfaces, and software-engineering workflows. A bottom annotation reads, “Requirements flow inward; technical practices enable compliance.”
context:
:::

Engineering teams do not operate in isolation. Team-level technical practices such as audit logging, bias testing, and explainable interfaces sit at the core of expanding organizational, industry, and regulatory structures, with requirements and legal mandates flowing inward across each boundary and the technical controls at the center supplying the evidence that external compliance rests on (@fig-governance-layers). The rest of this section works at that innermost ring, starting with who may reach the data at all.

title: Data Governance Documentation
caption: **Data Governance Documentation**: The populated Open Images Extended—More Inclusively Annotated People card organizes authorship, motivation, intended and unsafe uses, conjunctional use, and method caveats in one artifact. Recording permitted and prohibited uses makes the card reviewable governance evidence, though it does not establish compliance by itself. Adapted from the Open Images Extended—MIAP Data Card in @pushkarna2022.
alt: Structured data card for the Open Images Extended—More Inclusively Annotated People dataset. The card contains a dataset description and links, authorship and funding fields, motivations and intended-use fields, safety and unsafe-use warnings, conjunctional-use guidance, and method summaries with known caveats for object detection and fairness evaluation.
context:
Data-protection law reaches deeper into the pipeline than decision-level duties do, because its obligations attach to the data itself rather than to a decision. When a European user invokes an applicable right to erasure\index{Right to erasure!data lineage requirement} under GDPR, the voice assistant must determine which personal data and downstream artifacts are in scope and execute the appropriate workflow within the regulation's response deadlines [@gdpr2016]. These obligations become architecture constraints\index{Regulatory compliance!architecture constraints} in pipeline design, storage choices, and operational procedures. GDPR's data minimization principle\index{GDPR!data minimization principle}\index{Data minimization!privacy by design} requires limiting collection and retention to what is necessary for stated purposes. Article 15 access rights cover personal data undergoing processing and specified information about that processing, not every artifact merely associated with a user.

Voice assistants operating globally face overlapping regulatory regimes because requirements vary by jurisdiction and apply differently based on user age and data sensitivity. GDPR cross-border-transfer rules\index{Data localization!cross-border transfer} permit transfers through adequacy decisions, appropriate safeguards, or limited derogations rather than imposing categorical data localization. These rules can still drive regional storage, replication, and processing choices. A structured data card\index{Data card!compliance documentation} turns these operational metadata requirements into reviewable fields. The card in @fig-data-card, adapted from the Open Images Extended (MIAP) specification [@pushkarna2022], partitions authorship, primary motivations, explicit safety prohibitions (such as forbidding age or gender classification), and methodological caveats. Although documenting these boundaries does not alone guarantee statutory compliance, it provides the verifiable baseline necessary for pipeline ingestion checks.

Regrouped by the four parts in which they were introduced, the principles form a cycle rather than a pipeline (@fig-invariants-cycle). The deployment principles (9–13) turn runtime telemetry into evidence that sends work back to the data foundations, so each production lesson becomes the starting condition of the next design pass. The conservation-of-complexity heuristic sits at the center of that cycle because every pass around it asks where the complexity displaced by the previous decision has landed. Along that return path, principles 9 through 13 expose the signals that trigger targeted remediations such as canary rollbacks, fallback heuristics, dataset augmentation, model retraining, or kernel retuning, so that failures are caught before they compound.

title: Storage Layouts
caption: **Storage Layouts**: Row-oriented formats group values by record, so the illustrated scan reads every field. Column-oriented formats group values by feature, so the illustrated scan reads only Age.
alt: Diagram contrasting row and column stores. The row store groups ID, Age, and Loc values by record and reads every column. The column store groups values by column and reads only Age.
context:
### Row and columnar formats {#sec-appdx-data-foundations-row-vs-columnar-formats-bca2}

The choice of file format determines how many bytes a query moves through the storage hierarchy. Row-oriented formats such as CSV and JSON store data record-by-record, so reading the `age` field still requires parsing every attribute in each row. This layout suits append-only logs but incurs steep overhead for feature filtering. Parquet stores compressed column chunks on disk, while Arrow provides a contiguous columnar in-memory and IPC representation. Parquet readers exploit *projection pushdown*\index{Projection pushdown} to fetch selected column chunks directly, and both formats support *vectorized processing*\index{Vectorization!columnar processing}. Where the row layout forces a wide scan across all fields (`ID`, `Age`, `Loc`), the columnar layout isolates the target `Age` chunk and avoids moving irrelevant attributes (@fig-row-vs-col). @Sec-data-engineering-formats-compression-partitioning-8b17 develops format choice as a lever on the data term of the iron law.

title: Tensor Broadcasting Rules
caption: **Tensor Broadcasting Rules**: A (3,1) column and a (1,4) row broadcast across complementary dimensions, producing the pairwise sums in a (3,4) result.
alt: Tensor A, a three-cell column labeled A0 through A2 with shape (3,1), plus tensor B, a four-cell row labeled B0 through B3 with shape (1,4), equals a (3,4) grid whose cells contain every Ai+Bj pair. Dashed cells and an annotation indicate that A and B are read through stride-0 views, so the inputs are not copied while the (3,4) result is allocated.
context:
**Broadcasting**\index{Broadcasting!definition} allows arithmetic operations on tensors of different shapes by comparing dimensions from right to left. Two dimensions are compatible when they are equal or when one of them is 1.

Adding a $(3, 1)$ column tensor ($\BroadcastColumnTensor$) to a $(1, 4)$ row tensor ($\BroadcastRowTensor$) expands both virtually across their complementary singleton dimensions and generates a $(3, 4)$ matrix of pairwise sums $\BroadcastColumnElement_i + \BroadcastRowElement_j$ (@fig-broadcasting-rules). Dashed cell boundaries mark result elements whose operands are read through stride-0 views, so neither input is copied; only the $(3, 4)$ output is allocated, and hardware repeatedly accesses identical input buffer addresses.

title: Backpropagation Computational Graph
caption: **Backpropagation Computational Graph**: Solid gray arrows carry the forward computation from input $\InputFeatureVector$ to loss $\LossFunction$, while dashed red arrows carry gradients backward along the same dependencies.
alt: A computational graph with four nodes labeled x, h, y-hat, and a calligraphic L denoting loss, connected left to right. Solid gray arrows show the forward pass with weights W1 and W2. Dashed red arrows curve backward showing gradient flow with partial derivative notation.
context:
Backpropagation[^fn-backprop-chain-rule] implements the chain rule efficiently through two passes: forward to compute outputs, backward to compute gradients. The gradient edges retrace forward dependencies, meaning each backward step requires intermediate activations retained from the corresponding forward operation. @Fig-backprop-graph traces these dual dataflow passes across a two-layer network: solid gray arrows stage forward activations ($\InputFeatureVector\to \HiddenActivation\to \PredictedOutput$) through weight parameters $\WeightMatrix_1$ and $\WeightMatrix_2$ to evaluate loss $\LossFunction$, while curved dashed red arrows propagate intermediate adjoints ($\frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \PredictedOutput}, \frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \HiddenActivation}, \frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \InputFeatureVector}$) in reverse order.

[^fn-backprop-chain-rule]: **Backpropagation**\index{Backpropagation!appendix refresher}: Short for "backward propagation of errors." The algorithm was independently discovered multiple times, by @werbos1974beyond and @linnainmaa1970representation for reverse-mode differentiation and by @rumelhart1986 for neural network training. Its key insight is that computing gradients for all parameters requires one backward pass through the graph rather than one pass per parameter. @Sec-appdx-algorithm-baur-strassen derives the constant-factor work bound and a representative dense-layer cost.

title: The Roofline Model
caption: **The Roofline Model**: The sloped memory-bandwidth ceiling and horizontal peak-compute ceiling meet at the ridge point. Plotting a workload by arithmetic intensity identifies which roofline ceiling applies.
alt: A plot with arithmetic intensity on the x-axis and performance on the y-axis. Two lines form a roofline shape: a diagonal line rising from the origin labeled memory bound, and a horizontal line labeled compute bound. They meet at the ridge point.
context:
The Roofline Model\index{Roofline model!appendix refresher} [@williams2009] bounds how fast a workload can run on a given hardware target. The answer depends on whether the workload runs out of compute or memory bandwidth first.

Every operation has an **arithmetic intensity**\index{Arithmetic intensity!appendix refresher}: the ratio of computations performed to bytes moved from memory. Matrix multiplication achieves high arithmetic intensity because each loaded element is reused across multiple multiply-accumulate steps. In contrast, element-wise operations like rectified linear unit (ReLU) exhibit low intensity because each element is fetched from memory, evaluated once, and written back. Plotting achievable performance against arithmetic intensity yields the roofline (@fig-roofline): a diagonal memory-bandwidth ceiling rises linearly from the origin until it meets the horizontal peak-compute ceiling at the ridge point. A workload's arithmetic intensity determines which ceiling governs execution, and therefore whether optimizations must target memory traffic or arithmetic throughput.

alt: Pyramid with four tiers, from top to bottom: registers, L1/L2/L3 cache, HBM/DRAM, and storage (SSD/disk). An upward arrow reads “Faster Speed, Lower Latency,” and a downward arrow reads “Larger Capacity, Lower Cost.”

### The memory hierarchy {#sec-appdx-machine-foundations-memory-hierarchy-2278}

Computer systems rely on tiered storage architectures because no single physical medium simultaneously provides massive storage capacity and the lowest access latency. Faster, smaller, and costlier tiers sit close to the arithmetic units; larger and cheaper tiers sit farther away (@fig-memory-hierarchy). When data movement sits on the critical execution path, staging tensors into the upper tiers avoids the orders-of-magnitude latency penalties of off-chip DRAM and persistent storage that @tbl-memory-ratios-ref quantifies.
